title: ★ The 50-Yard Line

reason: Gruber weighs in on the Huang and Nvidia scandal with real commentary.
content_html:
Ever since the Huang/Nvidia scandal erupted, I’ve been thinking about a short post I wrote back in March, under the headline “Jensen Huang Doesn’t Smell Anything”:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, during an on-stage interview at The Hill & Valley Forum last week, was asked “What do you see as America’s unique advantages that other countries don’t have?”

His answer, after taking a moment to think, “America’s unique advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump.”

Huang, newly appointed to the aforelinked President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, seemingly doesn’t smell the growing stink.

The stink was the historically low (and sinking) popularity to which Trump’s 2.0 presidency had sunk. Undeniable to anyone in touch with reality. Huang’s obsequious Trump-fellating answer to that question would have been eye-catching even a year prior, when Trump first rolled back into office with an aggressive agenda and a surplus of political capital from a clear election victory — but it was, frankly, a startling thing to say in March 2026. It makes a lot more sense, though, given what’s come to light in the last 10 days.

[Update: This event was in July 2025, not March 2026, but while I regret that error, my points stand.]

If you’re not paying close attention you might think Huang’s was the sort of answer any major tech CEO might have given. But it’s not. That was a really unusual thing for Huang to say, way out of line with how corporate leaders typically approach politics. The typical approach for large publicly held corporations is to avoid partisan politics. Advocate only for policies directly related to the company’s business, and otherwise stay out. The political winds change direction every few years. George Bush senior in 1988 was the last new president elected from the same party as the outgoing incumbent, and he only lasted one term. It makes no sense for a corporation that intends to continue thriving for more than the next few years to closely align itself with one party — unless they believe that party will remain in power for the foreseeable future, à la the FDR/Truman Democrats, who won five consecutive presidential elections from 1932 to 1948 (and seven out of nine through 1968).

One metaphor I use for politics is a football field. Democrats on the left, Republicans on the right. CEOs typically stay as close as they can to the 50-yard line in the middle of the field. That way, when an election puts the other party in power, they don’t have to move — they just need to turn around. That’s how someone like Tim Cook could maintain good relations with the White House from Obama to Trump to Biden back to Trump again. He just stayed close to midfield and turned around after each election.

Remaining as close as possible to political midfield under Trump required unseemly obsequious tribute, unprecedented in modern U.S. history. Million-dollar tickets to his inauguration. That ridiculous gold trophy. Embarrassing stuff. But that’s ultimately a reflection of Trump’s avarice, not the politics of Cook personally or Apple as a company. That was the price to stay on the 50-yard line. Cook has often repeated that his two personal heroes are Martin Luther King Jr. and Bobby Kennedy (senior, to be clear). He keeps portraits of both of them in his office. He never swapped them out for portraits of, say, Ronald Reagan. Apple never changed its internal policies or language regarding racial and LGBT equality. The Apple homepage never stopped celebrating Martin Luther King Jr. Day — even when it coincided with Trump’s second inauguration.

And yet Trump remains so enamored of Cook that he floated his name to succeed Huang at Nvidia. Tim Apple remains the apple of Trump’s eye. Yet Apple had nothing to change or apologize for when Biden came into office, nor will they again if, as now seems likely, Trump is succeeded in 2029 by a Democrat elected to clean up his kakistocratic kleptomaniacal mess. (Presumably Apple will gladly pony up at least another $25 million to restore the East Wing after Trump’s architecturally ungodly ballroom edifice is torn down.) And Apple certainly won’t need lawyers to defend them from charges of corruption and/or breaches of national security. Nvidia, not so much.

This is what we should want: business leaders who endeavor to stay out of partisan politics, not hopelessly enmesh themselves in it. Industry and politics cannot operate in isolation, but they should avoid intertwinement except where necessary. Great companies stand the test of time. That’s not feasible if you hitch your corporate wagon to one party or the other, no matter the political moment. We don’t think of Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola, or Berkshire Hathaway as being Democratic or Republican companies. You cannot chart their fortunes over time based on which party was in power in any given decade. You may well have strong political opinions that are far from the 50-yard line, on one side or the other. I do. But you shouldn’t look for those opinions to be validated by industry executives, any more than you should look for business and product-design decisions to be made by elected government officials. True American values put country over party when it comes to business. And, as Calvin Coolidge aptly put it, “The chief business of the American people is business.”

America does possess unique advantages that other countries don’t have. Personal liberties enshrined in our Bill of Rights. A vibrant, diverse, ever-changing melting pot of a citizenry. A strong tradition of the rule of law, placing no man above it. Competitive markets that allow new entrants to supplant entrenched incumbents. Any CEO worth their salt should have an answer to the question of America’s unique advantages that holds true no matter who, from which party, is currently president. And they should believe it.

What makes Huang’s answer so off-putting isn’t that it was so abjectly partisan — politically tone-deaf to the inevitability of Democrats coming back into power, and perversely obsequious to Trump personally — but that Donald Trump is the antithesis to the entire above list of things that actually give America unique advantages other countries don’t have. Trump and the MAGA movement are also decidedly American and uniquely so, but they represent what’s worst about America.

But I give Huang credit for honesty. Clearly, he believed what he said. Huang didn’t just stray from the 50-yard line — he broke for Trump’s end zone.

title: Apple and Other Outages
summary: Juli Clover (Hacker News, John Gruber): Apple has largely resolved outages affecting iCloud accounts, retail stores, and more, the company said in a statement to Bloomberg. Apple said the outages were due to an unspecified “internal update” and were not caused by a cyberattack. The company is working to get remaining systems online “as soon […]
reason: Tsai rounds up the Apple iCloud outage and the lessons from an internal update gone wrong.
content_html:
Juli Clover (Hacker News, John Gruber):

Apple has largely resolved outages affecting iCloud accounts, retail stores, and more, the company said in a statement to Bloomberg. Apple said the outages were due to an unspecified “internal update” and were not caused by a cyberattack. The company is working to get remaining systems online “as soon as possible.”

Developer services like notarization were down for another 5 hours or so after that—but, then, notarization seems to go down every week.

I don’t know whether it’s related, but around the time the outage started, my Apple Watch stopped functioning. It would only show a small, white analog clock, and I couldn’t get to the main watch face. Restarting didn’t help. This had never happened to me before with any Apple Watch. I had to erase it and restore from backup.

I also wonder whether there’s any connection with the other recent outages.

Yahoo News (Hacker News, Slashdot):

While U.S. officials continue to investigate last week’s nationwide ground stop that caused thousands of flights to be delayed or canceled, the Federal Aviation Administration said on Tuesday that it is pausing the installation of routers linked to the outage.

CNN (Hacker News):

The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.

AP (Hacker News):

Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

CNN (Hacker News):

A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at US airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a rare FAA ground stop that caused massive disruption.

Natalie Musumeci (Hacker News):

Charles Schwab’s website briefly went down for some users on Tuesday.

summary: Apple added a dedicated Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app with iOS 27, which you can read more about in Federico’s annual review. Now that same feature is set to come to the iPad. Earlier this week, Apple released developer beta two for the 27.3 OSes. I wrote about many of those upcoming changes […]
reason: Visual Intelligence comes to the iPad Camera app in the 27.3 betas.
content_html:
Apple added a dedicated Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app with iOS 27, which you can read more about in Federico’s annual review. Now that same feature is set to come to the iPad.

Earlier this week, Apple released developer beta two for the 27.3 OSes. I wrote about many of those upcoming changes earlier this week but missed the changes to the iPad’s Camera app. As with iOS, when you open the Camera app in iPadOS 27.3, there will be a dedicated Siri mode. Switch to the new mode and the shutter button becomes a Siri icon. Tap it, and Siri will analyze the scene, describing what it sees. From there, you can use your finger or an Apple Pencil to circle or scrub over individual items, activating Visual Intelligence to search Google, Amazon, and other Visual Intelligence-enabled apps. Here’s a quick demo of it on the latest iPad mini that I recently reviewed:

Visual Intelligence is one of those iOS and iPadOS features that I’ve had trouble remembering to use. However, as you can tell from the video, it works really well for things like recognizable products. I’m glad to see this coming to the iPad, especially the mini, which I’m much more likely to use as a camera for capturing my surroundings.

title: How I got my recipes on HomeView via Safari
summary: It’s close, but not perfect (note the blank center image). One of my disappointments in Apple’s app strategy for the HomeView is that its choice to not support third-party apps—except via CarPlay—freezes out an entire class of apps that should be right at home on the device: recipe apps.…
reason: Snell finds a clever workaround for recipes on HomeView and critiques Apple app strategy.
content_html:
One of my disappointments in Apple’s app strategy for the HomeView is that its choice to not support third-party apps—except via CarPlay—freezes out an entire class of apps that should be right at home on the device: recipe apps.

HomeView features a fun recipe browser inside Safari, but if all your recipes are stored in an app—my preference is Silvio Rizzi’s Mela—then they are locked out of HomeView.

Or are they?

Before I get to my solution to this issue, I want to tip my cap to the inspiration I received from other quarters. Stephen Robles, motivated to solve this same issue, built an entire recipe-keeper app for HomeView. And I heard from Aaron Gold, the developer of Saucepan, another recipe app that has figured out HomeView integration.

Here’s the long and short of it: If you want your recipes to show up on the HomeView, they need to be web pages that open in Safari on the HomeView. That’s the only pathway right now. Robles and Gold both solved this problem by building apps that upload recipe data to a web server that generates and opens a private URL in Safari, which you can then just AirDrop directly to the HomeView.

This is probably what every developer who wants to support HomeView right now will have to do.

That said, while I hope Rizzi is on the case, I wasn’t satisfied with waiting and I didn’t want to move house to a different app. So I decided to see if I could solve this problem another way, namely by building a solution that would encode the HTML exported natively by Mela and open it in Safari in a way that would be transferable to the HomeView.

Here’s the result: a Shortcut you need to add, and a single HTML wrapper page you need to download and put on a web server you have access to. Download them both here.

When you’re in Mela, open a recipe and then tap the … menu, then Share: HTML… and from the resulting share sheet, choose the shortcut Mela to HomeView. It will open the recipe by loading the recipes.html file at the URL you chose (when you put it on the web server you have access to, remember?) and then passing all the data from the recipe into that web page via encoded data appended to the URL in Safari. The HTML file is just a wrapper; all the recipe data is included in the URL.

Then when Safari opens, bring your device close to the HomeView and it’ll transfer it over and load it in Safari, complete with a button to enter HomeView’s Recipe mode.

There’s one catch: Try as I might, I couldn’t get Recipe mode to display the pretty “cover image” of a recipe. Apparently for that you need to load the image from a remote server, and for this simple approach I don’t want to encourage people to build an extensive web back-end that’s capable of accepting uploads. (You can do it, to be sure, and I might—but for this solution I wanted it to be as simple as possible. Frankly, I don’t love that you have to put an HTML file on a web server at all, but here we are.)

Anyway, that’s my solution—for today. I hope that Mela and other recipe apps will solve this with hacks similar to those of Robles and Gold in the short term, and that Apple will provide better access to third-party recipe databases in the long term.

title: 10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers

reason: A decade-old unauthenticated RCE in NGINX HTTP/2 is a big deal for nearly every server fleet.
content_html:
A flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in.

The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today.

F5, the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port.

Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg.

In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container.

Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today.

Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.

Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories. That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6.

Wiz PoC

NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory.

Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0.

Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup:

Flaw What it needs
CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 turned on
CVE-2026-123633HTTP/2, with requests passed to a backend server while the worker is running low on 
worker_connections
CVE-2026-123634A proxied server name built from variables, plus a server-side include (SSI) or 
mirror
subrequest to a location that looks up the same name
CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 turned on
CVE-2026-113425 NGINX used as a mail proxy

HTTP/2 is on where a 

listen
directive includes 
http2
, or where 
http2 on
is set. Running 
openssl s_client
with 
-alpn h2
against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads 
ALPN protocol: h2
if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2.

Fixes, Workarounds and Signs of Attack

These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5:

  • NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 to 1.31.8 (mainline): fixed in 1.31.9
  • NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6, including older branches such as 1.28: fixed in 1.30.7
  • NGINX Plus 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1: fixed in 37.3.0.1
  • NGINX Plus 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1: fixed in 37.0.8.1
  • NGINX Plus R34 to R36: no fix listed

Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes. On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1.

After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes.

The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants.

Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that 

nginx -v
reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory.

Xint PoC

The vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and 

mirror
directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks.

CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs.

On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set 

http2 off;
in each affected 
server
block and remove 
http2
from its 
listen
directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove 
http2
from the 
listen
directive, so 
listen 443 ssl http2;
becomes 
listen 443 ssl;
. Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the 
openssl
check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2.

Until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line 

install sctp /bin/false
to a 
.conf
file in 
/etc/modprobe.d/
. That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel.

For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own.

Rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis. The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail.

The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the 

avx512f
and 
avx512vl
features.

Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post.

Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report.

Google News,

title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
summary: New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google's vice […]
reason: Big school districts push back on Google forcing Gemini features, a notable AI adoption fight.
content_html:
New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search

Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

content_html:
This week, a very El Niño-like atmospheric pattern is bringing needed precipitation to central and northern California.

Reservoirs are filling, and a substantial snowpack will accumulate over the higher terrain of the Golden State.  Good skiing with a week.

But the weather gods have not forgotten us.    The large-scale pattern will shift this weekend,  bringing substantial precipitation and mountain snow to our region as well.

Let's look at the latest forecast!

Over the next 72 hours (through Saturday morning), California will be quite wet.  The watershead of the Colorado River will do well, in addition.


But subsequently, the precipitation shifts northward, with Oregon and Washington State enjoying substantial wet action (see below). 
This will continue the next 72 hr, with the Northwest coast being hit very hard. 
Northwest ducks will be happy.


What about snow?  

Over the next ten days, first the Sierra Nevada and then the Northwest mountains will get plenty of snow (see the 10-day totals below).  Skiing will begin at Whistler.


So why will precipitation shift from California to the Pacific Northwest?  

That is easy to explain by looking at the average upper-level (500 hPa pressure, about 18,000 ft) map, averaged over 5-day chunks.  

For the first five days, there is a low-pressure area off California, which directs the bulk of the precipitation south of us.  


But everything changes during the subsequent five days; the upper low moves offshore and to the north--a much wetter pattern for the Northwest.


You can see the change at the surface.  The sea-level pressure pattern at 4 PM today has a low off of southern CA.

Fast forward to Monday afternoon: a VERY potent low is predicted to be off our coast (below).   And many more lows are in our future.


Importantly, these storms are not making landfall and are staying out to sea... which is very much an El Nino configuration.   But much wetter for western Washington and British Columbia.

Some are very happy with the forecast

title: The trouble with serendipity
summary: Many scientific discoveries didn’t happen the way you think.
reason: Works in Progress on how scientific discoveries really happen, a big-ideas read.
content_html:
Saloni Dattani explores accidental discoveries in history, and comes away learning that scientists’ lives were messier than she expected.

This is a column: a lighter piece from the Works in Progress extended universe, designed to be enjoyed in print. If you’d like to opt out of columns, or any other section, you can do so here.

People love accidental discoveries. Penicillin’s discovery by Alexander Fleming is a classic example. Fungal spores wafted in through an open window, fell onto a plate of bacterial colonies, and dissolved them. Another is Louis Pasteur’s discovery of a chicken cholera vaccine, the second vaccine ever developed. After Pasteur left a broth overexposed to oxygen, it went stale. But he ran out of fresh broth, so used it anyway to study the effects of an infection, and found, surprisingly, that it protected the chickens. Or how about the discovery of X-rays? Wilhelm Röntgen was working with a cathode ray tube in a dark room when he suddenly noticed a screen glowing nearby, even though he’d wrapped the tube in cardboard.

Subscribe now

Though they’re great stories, I’ve come to believe none of them happened that way. Röntgen had his notes burned after his death, and the story is just a hypothesis. Pasteur was extremely secretive as well, and forbade his family from making his notes and letters public after his death. His grandson, however, did, and after poring over their contents, historians have found that the key experiments were done deliberately by Pasteur’s then-assistant Émile Roux while Pasteur was away for his daughter’s wedding.

And what about Fleming? His first paper describing penicillin in 1929 never says where the spores came from. Of course, it’s hard to see how he could have known, given they would have been microscopic. But Fleming first told the window story in an interview in 1945, sixteen years after his first report, and his colleagues testified the window was ‘seldom if ever opened’. They weren’t able to replicate the discovery as he described, either: penicillin would have needed to be present on the plate before the bacteria grew, because it blocks bacteria from building their cell walls, rather than killing them once they’ve grown.

Subscribe to print

Several people have tried to work out what really happened. Fleming’s would-be biographer Ronald Hare made dozens of attempts and found just one reliable way to reproduce the discovery that fit the facts. The spores, he argues, were an unusually productive strain; came from the lab of a fungal researcher on the floor below, rather than the window; settled on the plate roughly when Fleming seeded it with bacteria; Fleming forgot to incubate it; and all this happened during a cold spell in the summer that let the mold grow before the bacteria. Hare noted how much more serendipitous this sequence of events was: ‘the odds against the occurrence of the phenomenon become almost astronomical’, though he ultimately believed it. While writing this column, I read through many of his notes and letters archived at the Wellcome Library and have come to agree with his view: Hare was exceedingly careful in corroborating the events from multiple people and sources from the time.

Part of the reason I find the popular stories fascinating is because it’s jarring to realize how little they’re based on. I do expect some stories of accidental discovery will survive the test of time. In medicine, for example, it’s fairly common to test a drug for one disease and find, unexpectedly, that it works for another: colchicine was used for centuries to treat gout before it was found effective against cardiovascular disease, and sildenafil (Viagra) was being tested for angina when its more famous effect was noticed. Side effects are difficult to predict.

Subscribe now

But I wonder why the popular versions have survived so long. Maybe they’re more enjoyable? They’re certainly easier to recount than the other explanations, which are convoluted. A fungal spore floating through an open window to reveal a world-changing antibiotic is a far better dinner party story than a meandering one involving several more coincidences you’ve probably already forgotten. Or the stories make scientists feel just like us: anyone can stumble upon a discovery, and then the challenge is merely to... spend years turning it into something useful?

‘Chance favors only the prepared mind’, as Pasteur put it. I think there’s something to it: the brilliance of these scientists isn’t necessarily in their initial discoveries, but in seeing their potential and doing something with them. Edward Jenner, for example, wasn’t the first to notice that cowpox infections protected against smallpox, but he documented it thoroughly and popularized the method, spreading smallpox vaccination worldwide.

But what bothers me is that calling these discoveries accidents is sometimes the opposite of reality. Pasteur and Roux, for example, carried out hundreds of experiments to find reliable methods to create new vaccines – the popular framing is actively misleading and diminishes their work.

My friend Niko McCarty recently dug into other famously serendipitous discoveries in biology, such as those of green fluorescent protein and nanopore sequencing, and explained they came from systematic trial and error. He also describes the idea of ‘engineered serendipity’: in optogenetics, for example, ‘the key breakthrough came about because the inventors wrote down the exact requirements they were looking for [...] and then enumerated, or wrote down, all the ways they could possibly imagine to make this happen’. It makes me wonder if learning how they really happened could help understand how to make more discoveries systematically.

Yet I’m still left with questions. Why credit chance events instead of hard work? Why hide or burn your notebooks?

Messiness, mistakes, and privacy come to mind. But here’s another theory: competition and rivalry. Gerald Geison, a historian of Pasteur, suggests the method he ultimately used to develop chicken cholera vaccines was ‘remarkably simple’ and could be applied to other diseases too: ‘had he revealed immediately the method of attenuation through exposure to ordinary air, Pasteur might have faced a host of competitors in the search for other vaccines’. Pasteur was probably the best-paid scientist in France at the time, and sold his inventions commercially. His secrecy might have been rational: patents weren’t allowed on medicines in France then, so keeping the method secret would have helped him maintain his monopoly on producing them. Pasteur was so cagey that he didn’t allow his collaborators to take notes, took his notebooks with him when he traveled, and published his methods (without much detail) only months after announcing his discoveries.

Subscribe to print

Meanwhile, Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays and had his notes burned after his death, had been in a long dispute with another scientist, Philipp Lenard. Lenard had spent years researching cathode rays before him, and shared his methods and discharge tube with Röntgen. Once Röntgen became famous, Lenard accused him of having robbed him of the discovery. That dispute, historians suggest, could have motivated the note-burning, but it’s hard to know without being able to read them. (Incidentally, Émile Roux, too, had his notes burned periodically, and it’s only because Pasteur’s were released that we know what happened at all.)

Science seems like it should be above the messiness. It’s an institution we’ve built to guard against our biases. But it’s also just people – who forget, hide their notebooks from their colleagues, burn their papers, and spend years fighting over who deserves credit. It’s shaped by rivalries, incentives, obsessions, and years of unglamorous work, most of which is forgotten. That, to me, makes it far more interesting than a story about an open window.

Saloni Dattani is an editor at Works in Progress.

reason: UK tribunal ruling keeps Apple's fight over an encryption backdoor order largely public.
content_html:
Apple's challenge to a UK government demand for access to encrypted customer data can now be heard largely in public, after a tribunal rejected the Home Office's attempt to keep the order secret, according to the Financial Times.


The Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government had failed to demonstrate that confirming the demand would damage national security. The decision requires the Home Office to acknowledge that it served Apple with a technical capability notice (TCN), which is an order that can compel companies to make customer data accessible to UK security services, even when it is encrypted.

The government's position relied on its policy of neither confirming nor denying such notices. However, the tribunal found that disclosures to the media, including the Financial Times, and discussions with U.S. officials had already departed significantly from that policy.

In its judgment, the tribunal said the combined effect was that anyone following the dispute already knew Apple had received a TCN. It described the suggestion that official acknowledgment would threaten national security or give a malicious actor fresh information as "fanciful."

The ruling means that much of the legal action brought by Apple, alongside a separate challenge from Privacy International and Liberty, can proceed in open court.

Apple filed its latest legal challenge in July, following a second TCN. The Home Office had previously agreed to withdraw an earlier demand covering UK and U.S. customers after a dispute with the American government. The replacement notice is believed to focus on UK users specifically.

The dispute led Apple to stop offering Advanced Data Protection to new users in the UK in February 2025. The iCloud feature provides end-to-end encryption for additional categories of data, including device backups, photos, and notes, meaning Apple does not hold the keys needed to decrypt them.

UK users who had not already enabled ADP can no longer turn it on. Apple says it cannot switch the feature off on their behalf, so it can remain active on accounts where users previously enabled it and have not turned it off. The company said affected users will be given a period to disable ADP themselves to continue using ‌iCloud‌, but a deadline has still not been provided.

Without ADP, those additional categories of ‌iCloud‌ data use standard protection, under which Apple holds the encryption keys and can provide data in response to valid legal demands. iMessage and FaceTime remain end-to-end encrypted, as do categories protected by default, such as passwords and Health data.

The tribunal will now be able to hear much of the arguments over the government's encryption demands in public, with the legality of those demands still to be decided. Privacy International lists the substantive hearing for its separate challenge as scheduled for December 2026.

title: YoLink sensors are powering my key household alerts
summary: I was at Casey Liss‘s house over the weekend, sitting in his living room, when suddenly I heard a chime and a voice said, out of nowhere: “The wash is done.”…
reason: Snell on using YoLink sensors for household alerts, a thoughtful home tech piece.
content_html:
I was at Casey Liss‘s house over the weekend, sitting in his living room, when suddenly I heard a chime and a voice said, out of nowhere: “The wash is done.”

It turns out that Casey has connected an array of sensors to his Home Assistant setup, and somehow his family accepts that occasionally a disembodied voice will shout out home status information. (It’s not as subtle as his other approach.)

What’s wilder is that the box Casey’s using to do this is actually one I have in my own home! It’s a YoLink Speaker Hub, which I bought along with three leak sensors (affiliate link; I bought a three-pack of sensors with the hub for $60) a year and a half ago. And while I haven’t automated my speaker hub to announce things (yet!), I realized I haven’t sufficiently sung the praises of these YoLink sensors.

In short: They are very good, with tremendous range and battery life, and extremely easy to install. You don’t actually need anything like Home Assistant to use them—they come with their own, entirely functional app for configuration and alert purposes.

The leak sensors themselves are tiny plastic pucks you just put in potential trouble spots—for me, that’s under the kitchen sink, next to the washing machine, and next to the condensate pump that doubles as the outlet for my dehumidifier in the winter months. When they register a leak, I get an emergency notification on my phone and (optionally) the Speaker Hub can make an unmissable alert noise.

We’ve previously had under-sink and washing-machine disasters, so this was an easy purchase for me. And since I installed them, I’ve been alerted once about a serious issue—the drain hose from my dehumidifier had come out of the pump housing and was dripping freely.

Casey’s also taking advantage of the long battery life and range of YoLink’s system to do things like use contact sensors to alert him when his mail has been delivered, and the company offers a wild array of sensors that work with the hub.

And, yes, once you plug the Speaker Hub into Home Assistant, you can drive its built-in audio features, which include built-in text-to-speech, a library of alert tones, and even custom MP3 sounds, from any automation happening in your house. (Casey’s laundry alerts are, impossibly, not from smart appliances, but from inline energy-consumption monitors he’s attached to his washer and dryer.)

If you’re so inclined, you can really go to town with these sensors. But if you just want basic operation, such as making sure that the next time your sink leaks it’s not a total disaster, I can’t recommend the YoLink sensors and hub highly enough.

title: Voyager 1 Now One Light-Day from Earth
summary: Yesterday was a big day: The Voyager 1 spacecraft, traveling for nearly 50 years, will soon cross a mile marker reached by no other human-made object — one light-day away from Earth. That’s the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equaling about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion …
reason: Hackett on Voyager 1 nearing one light-day from Earth, a hopeful science moment.
content_html:
Yesterday was a big day:

The Voyager 1 spacecraft, traveling for nearly 50 years, will soon cross a mile marker reached by no other human-made object — one light-day away from Earth. That’s the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equaling about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), a point that Voyager 1 will reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST.

One of the most interesting things — among many — about the Voyager probes is their on-board gold records.

Robert Pearlman dug into them for Ars Technica:

In the one light-day that humanity’s most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.

Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter’s moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a “commemorative phonograph record,” in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.

About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs’ overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.

“So much has been written about the contents of the record—the message in the bottle, so to speak—whereas I was more interested in the hardware, the bottle itself, because so very little is known about that,” Swanson, former chief historian for NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston and founding editor of Quest: The History of Spaceflight Quarterly, said in an interview.

title: Dancing with the trophy shortage
summary: It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on. But this skips the key question: What’s it for? The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other […]
reason: Seth Godin on chasing trophies versus the real work.
content_html:
It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on.

But this skips the key question: What’s it for?

The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other team.

Your favorite episode of the Mel Robbins show might not be the one that got the most views. And of course, the best video on YouTube is unlikely to be the one that went the most viral. That’s simply the easiest to measure.

High school sports seems to be about solving the trophy shortage, but is that what it should be for? Are all the other teams and all their athletes failures? Or is it simply a shortcut that lets the coach off the hook when they hesitate to do the hard work of developing their students?

If it’s easy to measure, it might not be the thing you ought to be measuring. In fact, it probably isn’t.

title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: What’s new in Azure, the platform purpose-built for AI
summary: At Microsoft Ignite, we're sharing what's new across every layer of the platform. New capabilities spanning compute, storage, and networking let you run AI at scale with the control of your own infrastructure, without having to build, secure, and operate all of it yourself. The post Microsoft Ignite 2026: What’s new in Azure, the platform purpose-built for AI appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog .
reason: Overview of Azure announcements at Ignite, relevant to an Azure security PM.
content_html:
Azure at Microsoft Ignite 2026: The headlines
  • Azure AI core: AI on infrastructure you control.
  • Azure Cobalt 200: Our highest-performing general-purpose virtual machines (VMs).
  • Azure Catalyst: Agent-led modernization from plan to code.
  • Agentic cloud operations: Agents that keep your cloud running well.
  • Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB: PostgreSQL for AI apps and analytics.
  • Fabric apps: Governed apps built on trusted data.
  • Microsoft IQ: Context for every agent.

Over the past year, my conversations with customers have changed. A year ago, the question was which model to choose. Now it’s how to put agents to work on the processes that run the business, and how to trust them to do it.

With the same frontier models available to everyone, the advantage comes from what no one else has: your context. It’s how your business runs, what your people know, and the systems and data you’ve spent years building. That’s your IQ. It’s your intellectual property, so it should stay yours, and it should work wherever your people and agents do. Our job is to make every layer beneath your agents better, from the infrastructure that runs them and the estate they act on to the apps they power and the business context that tells them how your company works.

Azure is the foundation of Frontier Transformation. We engineer Azure as one system, so the knowledge an agent needs stays governed and the security you use to protect your people extends to the agents acting for them. And because we’re evolving the open, cloud-native platform you already rely on, you don’t have to start over.

See what Azure can do for your business

As Satya Nadella shared at Microsoft Build in June, we added more datacenter capacity in 18 months than in Azure’s first decade. Combined with more regions than any other cloud provider, you can scale your AI workloads globally with confidence as demand grows.

This week at Microsoft Ignite, we’re sharing what’s new across every layer of the platform. New capabilities spanning compute, storage, and networking let you run AI at scale with the control of your own infrastructure, without having to build, secure, and operate all of it yourself. Azure Catalyst brings agent-led modernization together in one experience from estate to code.

PostgreSQL now has two homes at Microsoft: Azure HorizonDB, generally available for mission-critical scale, and the new Fabric HorizonDB, which connects your PostgreSQL apps to analytics and AI. And Fabric apps, now generally available, let your teams turn trusted enterprise data into working apps.

We’re also introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform that helps you build your own IQ and put it to work in every app and agent. It also gives your teams a path on Azure to build, run, and continuously improve those agents.

Run AI at scale with the control you choose

It starts with the infrastructure that runs your agents. As they take on real work, you should be able to run them on your terms, with your choice of models, your data, and where they run. That control lets you find the right balance of performance and cost for each workload and adapt as models and needs change.

But control comes with real work and risk. Platform teams end up assembling and operating much of the AI stack themselves and stretching GPUs to keep up with shifting demand. Agents that reach models, tools, and data and run code on their own open new security gaps, putting sensitive data at risk.

Teams want the control of running their own AI infrastructure without taking on all the manual toil of building, securing, and operating it.

Building the AI core on Azure

That’s what we’re bringing to Azure. New capabilities across compute, storage, and networking come together as one AI foundation, so you keep control of your models and workloads while Azure takes on the work underneath. Build AI with Microsoft Foundry in a fully managed experience and run it at scale with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) when you need more control over performance, security, and cost.

Ignite session: AI infrastructure from cloud to Edge

Watch now ↗

Azure sets up and tunes the infrastructure for you, so your teams spend less time on configuration and more time moving models and agents into production. Workloads are placed based on available capacity, so your GPU investment goes further as demand grows. Security is enforced centrally across agents, models, and tools, giving security teams consistent controls wherever agents run. And because it’s built on open-source projects, your workloads stay portable, including to your own servers outside Azure, keeping your options open as your needs change.

The result is AI that scales with your business, on infrastructure you control.

To hear how organizations are operating AI at scale, join Mark Russinovich and Pavan Davuluri in the innovation session “AI Infrastructure from cloud to edge.”

Strengthening every layer of your AI estate with Azure Cobalt 200

Agents reason, make decisions, and run continuously, and that’s reshaping what cloud infrastructure needs to deliver. That’s why we design Azure as one system, from silicon to servers to services. We pair our own Maia and Cobalt chips with the latest from NVIDIA and AMD, so every workload runs on the right silicon for the job. Our strategy focuses on building performance, efficiency, and security into every layer. The result is AI that’s faster and more economical to run at scale, on a roadmap you can plan around.

Ignite session: cobalt 200…

Watch now ↗

Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines, our highest-performing general-purpose VMs, are now generally available. Designed from the ground up for scale-out, cloud native, and agentic AI workloads, these VMs deliver up to 50% better CPU performance compared to our Cobalt 100 VMs. Together with Maia, they give you an infrastructure you can plan around.

Read about the latest Azure Cobalt updates in this blog

Agent-led modernization and operations, from estate to code

Agents are only as useful as the systems they can act on. Much of what makes your company unique is built into your applications and databases and years of business logic your teams rely on. Modernizing puts existing apps and data to work in new AI-powered experiences, helps teams ship faster, and lowers the cost and risk of running older systems, creating a more adaptable foundation for growth.

Getting there isn’t easy. Modernizing can mean mapping complex systems and changing code that few people fully understand. Keeping the estate running well means sorting through constant signals with little knowledge on what matters most. And as agents take on more of that work, teams need to let them act while keeping the oversight your business requires.

That’s why we’re bringing agents to both, from estate to code. Azure Catalyst helps you modernize applications, code, and databases from plan to execution. And new capabilities in Azure Copilot, Azure SRE Agent, and Azure Monitor help keep your cloud and databases running well, with people in control.

Modernize for AI with Azure Catalyst

Azure Catalyst is a new unified experience for agentic modernization. It brings discovery, planning, migration, modernization, and code intelligence together, so IT teams and developers work from the same plan across infrastructure, applications, and data. Azure Catalyst modernizes the technology you already have into a foundation for AI, putting the business logic in your existing applications to work in new AI-powered experiences and agentic business processes.

Ignite session: rethink modernization…

Watch now ↗

For IT teams, Azure Catalyst agent extends from migration planning into deeper modernization and execution. For developers, GitHub Copilot modernization carries that plan into code in the tools they already use, with agent governance rulebooks and bring-your-own-model support that customizes your modernization project to the specifications of each business. And Azure Catalyst delivers a deeper understanding of how enterprise applications work, so teams can assess the impact of changes, modernize faster, and find where legacy processes could be reimagined with AI.

Ignite session: modernize faster with ai…

Watch now ↗

Modernization can also close security gaps. End-of-support runtimes, unpatched dependencies, and aging code widen your threat surface. Azure Catalyst works with Microsoft Security to fix that: Microsoft Perception and MDASH rank vulnerabilities across your estate and code, Azure Catalyst identifies vulnerable code and databases to modernize first, and GitHub Copilot turns those findings into fixes in the same pass. Each app comes out more secure than it went in.

Learn more about Azure AI foundation and Azure Catalyst in this blog

Keep your cloud running well with agentic operations

As applications scale across hybrid infrastructure, microservices, and AI workloads, leading organizations are moving to operating models where insight flows directly into action. That’s the idea behind agentic operations: AI agents, guided by your intent, continuously observe, reason, and help take action across the cloud lifecycle. Signals feed coordinated workflows that improve performance, cost, and reliability as systems run, with people kept in control.

At Microsoft Ignite, we’re bringing that model to more of your estate. Azure Copilot‘s deployment agent, now generally available, helps you go from requirements described in natural language to deployed cloud workloads. You can even extend agentic operations to Oracle and SAP with Azure Workload Center, now in limited preview.

Ignite session: put ai agents to work…

Watch now ↗

Azure SRE Agent brings agentic operations into secure production environments, with new enterprise controls in preview, while Microsoft Entra Agent ID and Agent 365 give central teams a consistent way to discover, govern, and audit agents throughout their lifecycle. We’re also giving agents richer data and understanding so they can detect issues earlier, diagnose problems faster, and take more effective action. Azure Monitor health models, now generally available, give agents a real-time view of your application architecture and business priorities, so they can recommend fixes.

Learn more about agentic operations in this blog

Build the next generation of AI apps

Then there are the apps your agents power, where business data becomes business value. The question for every organization is how quickly it can move from idea to an app the entire business can rely on. Today, the people building AI apps span the whole organization. Developers are creating mission-critical systems and new apps with agents, while teams across the business are describing the app they need in Copilot. Each needs something different from the platform, but every app needs to connect to business data and run under governance IT can trust.

We’re building one foundation for all of them, and it starts with PostgreSQL, the database of choice for a growing share of developers. With Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB, you can run PostgreSQL wherever your apps need it, from mission-critical systems to analytics and AI. Fabric apps builds on that foundation, so teams can turn business data into working apps, whether they start in code or in conversation.

Power your AI apps with PostgreSQL on Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB

The apps developers build now reason over data, call models, and act for users, so the database underneath has to bring transactions, vectors, and AI together at mission-critical scale. Azure HorizonDB, now generally available, is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database built for that work. It delivers millisecond latency with built-in vector indexing, so your apps can find, reason over, and act on data in one place. Enterprise-grade security comes built in, and developers can work in tools they already know, including GitHub Copilot and Visual Studio Code.

ignite session: data foundations for modern apps…

Watch now ↗

We’re also extending the power of PostgreSQL directly into Microsoft Fabric. Fabric HorizonDB, now in public preview, brings a serverless, Fabric-native PostgreSQL experience alongside SQL database in Fabric and Cosmos DB in Fabric. By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps.

To simplify database management across environments, Database Hub in Fabric is now generally available. It provides a unified experience to discover, monitor, and manage databases across Azure, on-premises environments, and Fabric, with Fabric Copilot highlighting what needs attention.

Read the latest Microsoft Databases announcements in this blog

Turn ideas into governed enterprise-ready apps with Fabric apps, now generally available

Great ideas for apps come from every corner of the business, and with Copilot, people can build one in minutes. But taking it from prototype to production on trusted data remains the biggest hurdle. Fabric apps, now generally available, bring together the backend services applications need with direct access to trusted data in Fabric, built-in security, and enterprise governance. Developers and coding agents build in code with open-source tools, and Fabric provisions everything from databases to authentication, with no infrastructure to manage. This makes it easier to turn ideas into enterprise-ready applications that can scale across the organization.

ignite session: build like a startup…

Watch now ↗

We’re also extending Fabric’s role as the data foundation for AI-powered applications. With the new Microsoft Copilot integration, now in Frontier public preview, anyone can describe the app they need and bring it to life, with the option to use Fabric as a ready-to-use data backend providing databases, storage, and data APIs. We’re also introducing Copilot Credits as a new usage-based billing option for Microsoft Fabric, providing greater flexibility alongside existing capacity-based options.

Power BI creators can now build more than static reports. With a new agentic app creation experience in Power BI Desktop, now in preview, they can turn their existing semantic models into interactive apps that capture input, update data, and support operational workflows.

Learn more about Fabric apps in the Ignite Microsoft Fabric blog

Ground every agent in your business context with Microsoft IQ

Most organizations already have the knowledge their agents need. It lives in the semantic models your analysts built in Power BI, the documents and procedures your teams rely on, the conversations happening across Microsoft 365, and the systems of record you run every day, like SAP and Oracle. The problem is that it’s scattered, so every new agent starts from zero and every team rebuilds the same context.

That’s why we’re introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform for building your organization’s IQ. It brings together Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, Web IQ, and more than 350 connectors, so the knowledge your agents need is captured once, governed in one place, and reused by every agent and app.

At the heart of Microsoft IQ are new business plugins, now available as part of the Frontier program. Business plugins turn what your teams know into trusted context, skills, and tools that anyone across the business can reuse. Take a supply chain disruption. A business plugin can tell an agent to use the components and orders semantic model in Fabric IQ to find the affected orders, the supplier contracts in Foundry IQ to check late-delivery terms, and Work IQ to find who owns the decision. Your domain experts write it once, and every agent across the organization inherits it.

Teams can also reuse proven evaluations across agents instead of rebuilding them. The foundation underneath Microsoft IQ brings Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Fabric together in one path, built on Azure, to build, run, and continuously improve agents. And Agent 365 gives IT one place to observe, govern, and secure them.

ignite session: Harnessing Your IQ…

Watch now ↗

Your IQ stays yours, and it isn’t locked into one assistant. The same context and business plugins reach your agents wherever they run, in Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT, through model context protocol (MCP) and APIs. Your permissions and governance go with it. Agents can also draw on the business context in your systems of record, like SAP and Oracle, so they work from the data your teams already rely on. Learn more about Oracle’s latest integrations with Microsoft IQ.

See how the Australian Energy Market Operator uses Microsoft IQ to help keep Australia’s power grid secure:

Nearly 60,000 customers already use Microsoft IQ today. And because every agent builds on the same context, each one you add makes the next one better.

Learn more about Microsoft IQ in this blog

Experience these innovations at Microsoft Ignite

Every agent you build is only as good as what it knows about your business. That’s why we’re making sure your IQ, the context that makes your company unique, is available to your agents across every layer of Azure, with governance and security built in. It stays yours, and its value grows with everything you build on it.
