title: iPhone Duo Camera Review: Form Brings Function
summary: While it lacks the iPhone 18 Pro's camera, the Duo still captures amazing photos. If you're considering the Duo but take iPhone photography seriously, the ultimate question is whether the small tradeoffs are worth what the Duo gives in return.
feed: Lux — iPhone camera apps, camera reviews and more
reason: iPhone Duo camera review from an iPhone photography specialist.
content_html:
iPhone Duo Camera Review: Form Brings Function

With its debut, the iPhone Duo was dinged by critics for having a camera system that's a step-down from the iPhone Pro. It seemed like this wasn't the camera to use on once-in-a-lifetime trips. I guess Halide users didn't get the memo.

While it lacks the iPhone 18 Pro's camera, the Duo still captures amazing photos. If you're considering the Duo but take iPhone photography seriously, the ultimate question is whether the small tradeoffs are worth what the Duo gives in return.

This review is not an epic trip across the globe. We're saving that for the 18 Pro. Instead, we're taking a trip to the New York Botanical Gardens for its annual Holiday Train Show.

The show featuring 200 miniatures, carved from real plant parts, which recreate famous New York landmarks

With computational photography, it's easy for software to compensate for poor hardware. That's why we're starting this review with photos that skip the shenanigans, so we can see how the hardware stands on its own.

These are very good cameras, which makes sense, as they're about on-par with the iPhone 17 Pro.

And Now For the Mandatory AI Discussion

None of the above photos were touched by the new AI photo editing that Apple launched in iOS 27. I have to admit, I have an aversion to this stuff. Maybe I just prefer the honesty of flaws. That said, I won't fault you for using AI to alter photos you share with friends and family.

At the train exhibit, there were two cases where the cleanup tool could save the day. I gave it a whirl, and wow, it's come a long way. Can you tell what was altered here?

There used to be a guy at the door in the background. The clean enough tool is now smart enough to fill in the occluded door panel.

In another instance, someone snuck into my frame and I didn't notice. I try my best to avoid photographing strangers, but sometimes I get tunnel vision and this happens.

Is it acceptable to use clean up to protect the privacy of someone else's kid?

Regardless, the cleanup tool has come a long way. I was used to smudgy slop, but with iOS 27, the results look seamless.

The Reframe tool makes me feel even more uncomfortable, but also gave me a good laugh. I tried to reframe this miniature of the botanical gardens, the AI confused it with the real botanical gardens, and it inserted a New York skyline.

And then we get to Extend. Please forgive me.

I spent an hour staging and lighting a "hero" photo for this review. No matter how I positioned the camera, even standing on a ladder, I couldn't get quite the composition I wanted. It felt too tight.

I began wondering how Apple Photos' Extend would handle it.

Well, I'll be damned.

I feel dirty, and I don't know why. Would I feel better if I didn't use AI, and I extended the shot in Photoshop by hand? I don't have answers. Right or wrong, Apple's AI photo editing has gotten really good.

This concludes all the AI you'll find in this post.

The Hardware and Low Light

When comparing the main camera of the Duo and Pro, it all comes down to light. Based on a teardown by Wekihome, the Duo's main camera sensor is 30% smaller than the iPhone 18 Pro, and its aperture opens to ƒ/1.48 compared to the Duo's ƒ/1.6. In total, you're looking at around 75% less light on the Duo.

The Duo uses the first generation sensor shift stabilization, while the 18 Pro uses the second generation introduced way back in the 14 Pro. That makes the Duo on-par with the budget iPhone models. It's safe to assume that this wasn't a cost cutting measure, but a technical requirement to keep the device thin.

In theory, you should expect the iPhone Duo to use higher ISO. Will this lead to more noise reduction and that "watercolor look" that screams iPhone photo? In practice, I didn't see this.

Consider this spectacular rainbow at dusk, skipping over Apple's noise reduction.

Zoom into the sky, and there you go.

This photo was ƒ/1.6, ISO 160, 1/60 exposure. This is about what you can expect shooting an interior at night. I think it's pretty good! I think sensor noise became much less of a concern on iPhones with the introduction of the 48 megapixel sensor, which "bin" adjoining pixels to cut noise.

Here's the same shot with the first party camera. It uses the 'Standard' photographic style, with default settings, and then tweaked in the Photos app to better match Halide's shot.

If we zoom into the sky, we see it's completely noise free.

But once you zoom in details, things feel a bit plastic.

A good friend of mine who works in visual effects describes noise as, "analog dithering." In the real world, whenever light hits a photo sensor, there's a natural randomness that orbits around the truth. When you leave the noise in an image, your brain pieces together the fine details, even better than software. When you apply aggressive noise reduction, you wipe that information.

Noise comes down to taste, and Apple defaults to heavy noise reduction. However, with the latest version of photographic styles, they added a "grain" option to bring back texture. Let's turn it on.

From the looks of it, Apple is adding a synthetic layer of grain after noise reduction, as opposed to preserving the original noise. If that's really what's happening, I strongly disagree with this choice.

I don't think there's anything wrong with letting users bump up texture. That's why we give you that option in Halide.

But if you're going to have noise, I think you should preserve the original noise. Noise reduction strips information, and adding new noise afterwards amounts to an optical illusion. You're robbing Peter to pay Paul.

Anyway, if you want to reduce the noise in low light, the Duo benefits from its size and inertia. Open it up, hold it with both hands, and brace it against your body. I was able to slow down by an extra two stops and still get acceptable shots.

Unfortunately, you're going to have to use a third-party app to do this. Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo lacks "Pro Controls" in the first-party app. That's too bad, because slow shutters are fun.

We round out our sensor discussion by flipping things around. All front-facing cameras have the same sensor size as the iPhone 17 and 18 Pro. The exact size is… complicated. While Apple describe the front sensor as square, it's actually octagonal! You just don't see the awkward corners because iOS crops your photos into portrait or landscape.

The inner front-facing camera is worse off because it's hidden behind the display, which is like taking a photo behind a screen door. It's going to cost light and detail.

Apple does not allow RAW capture from the inner front-facing camera. Developers can only access the final, processed image. Maybe Apple knows that the unprocessed image is so bad that it's a waste of a photographer's time.

The inner front-facing camera is fine for FaceTime calls. If you want to take a good self-portrait, you should at least use the outer front-facing camera. Better yet, unfold the Duo and use the back-facing camera.

The Tele-phant In the Room

So the biggest omission, and most valid criticism of the Duo, is the lack of a telephoto camera. Will you miss it?

If you only shoot with Apple's camera app, you probably use the telephoto camera less often than you think. When there isn't enough light, or you try to capture something too close for it to focus, Apple's camera app quietly switches over to the main camera and crops its results. It doesn't matter if you had the 4× button selected.

Fortunately, Apple's camera app saves metadata telling you the actual focal length used. This makes it easy to check in Apple Photos using a Smart Album.

In the last two years, I've shot over 5,000 photos, and about 12% used the telephoto lens, and a good chunk were purely test photos for developing Halide. This made me comfortable trying the Duo as my daily driver, and in the last few weeks, I haven't had a single moment like, "Man, I wish I had a telephoto right now!" Then again, I've been pretty busy working on these Halide updates, so I haven't had time for any scenic trips.

The Lack of Pro Formats

I will say that the Duo's biggest weakness is the inability to capture ProRAW. ProRAWs give you incredible latitude when editing high dynamic range scenes like this one.

If we zoom in, you'll notice sensor noise.

Unlike the low-light example earlier, here we have too much light in our scene. If we expose the shot to raise the shadows, we'll very likely clip details in highlights. We have to starve the shadows of light, which brings with it noise.

On the iPhone Pro, this is no problem. Deep Fusion takes multiple exposures, and packages it into a ProRAW for editing flexibility. Unfortunately, the Duo (and the rest of the non-Pro iPhones), only support native, Bayer RAWs. I'll also note that Night Mode is only available in the first party camera app, and it doesn't shoot Bayer RAW.

That's a longwinded way of saying that when shooting high dynamic range scenes, or using Night Mode, you are strictly limited to Apple's photographic styles.

Whether that's a dealbreaker is a matter of personal taste. Apple's photographic styles are not my cup of tea, but if you love them, great. I'm mostly disappointed that they're your only option, when I don't know a technical reason for it. ProRAW debuted in 2020 on iPhones with significantly less memory and processing power.

That said, third-party apps like Project Indigo build their own computational photography pipelines from scratch. It won't be consistent with Apple's camera app, but it might be a fine substitute when you have these itches.

The same can't be said of Apple Log, which is only available on the Pro lineup of iPhones. Even if a developer wanted to build their own version of Apple Log, Apple doesn't provide the APIs to do it.

Judging the Tradeoffs

The iPhone Duo is a great camera that allows you to produce amazing photos. It just isn't an iPhone Pro. In return, you get the benefits of an iPhone Duo. Is the Duo for you?

Since I began using the Duo as my daily driver three weeks ago, a number of strangers have struck up conversation asking what I think of it. This isn't the same level of curiosity as the first iPhone, but there's definitely interest. If you got this far into the review, clearly you're considering it. For all its 1.0 flaws, I really dig this device. I think it'll be popular. I just don't think it's the next step of phones.

You came for a camera review, so let's use a camera metaphor…

That's 35mm film. It dominated mass market photography until the move to digital in the 2000s. If someone says "film," you probably picture 35mm.

When NASA needed to capture the moon landing, they reached for "medium format," which is about 60mm. That film requires bigger, chonkier cameras.

A normal iPhone is like 35mm camera, and it hits the perfect sweet spot between size and utility for most people. An iPad is medium format. It's great when you need to watch a movie or do some light productivity, but iPads are annoying to carry everywhere.

A few decades into mass market photography, we saw interesting experiments with transforming cameras. The Mamiya 6 had a collapsible lens design, bringing medium format to a portable form factor. In 1998, Hasselblad released the XPan, a bizarre camera that takes 35mm film, but let you capture photos as wide as shooting medium format.

These cameras didn't set the world on fire. They were expensive, and solved a niche problem. However, they were still profitable. These companies sold these products for years, and even released updates like the Mamiya 7 and XPan II. These cameras have developed a bit of a cult following.

Foldables will always be more expensive and bulkier than single screen phones. Still, using a Duo for the last three weeks, I discovered a new itch alongside the scratcher. It's amazing to shoot a photo and then edit it seconds later on a screen with abundant space.

Niche cameras can thrive because film follows standards. If cameras were like apps, then all the film companies would have to update their film stocks whenever a new camera comes out. This is exactly the challenge Apple faces.

Apple needs companies to take the time to optimize apps for the Duo. Nobody wants a situation like Instagram, who waited 15 years before launching their iPad app. Even worse, some apps were outright janky on the day of the Duo launch.

That's because lots of apps were built on decades-long assumptions about iPhone interfaces, such as toolbars sitting at the bottom of the screen. I don't fault anyone for coding their apps around reasonable assumptions, and even Halide looked wonky on launch day. My penance was working through the weekend to ship a fix by Monday.

Three weeks later, Apple says over 200,000 apps have been updated for compatibility. My bank's app is not one of them, but hey, big corporations move slow. For most apps, the transition should be fairly painless if you paid attention to the to the "adaptive" APIs Apple introduced well over a decade ago. I'd wager all the popular apps will be serviceable before you can just walk into an Apple Store and walk out with a Duo.

That said, there's a difference between building an app that works on the Duo, and building a great experience for the Duo. While Apple's design guidance is a great starting point, it's deliberately generic. It can't tell you how your app can make the most of the new form factor, so it feels more than an iPhone app blown up to a big screen.

Making the most of the Duo for Halide has been an iterative, but fun, experience. When it was unveiled, the first idea that came to mind was "waist-level viewfinder," similar to a Hasselblad or Rolleiflex.

By half-closing the Duo and swapping from right to left, you can shoot from the hip.

This has some ergonomic perks, like capturing your kids at eye-level without hunching over. Alternately, raise it above your head and look up, to get shots above crowds. Just please, please don't do that at concerts.

Some photographers find that changing their perspective gives them a fresh take on the art form. In portraiture, lowering the camera removes a barrier between you and your subject, and can lead to more candid results.

Another idea for the Duo was the ability to review your last photo side-by-side with the viewfinder.

Caught someone blinking or looking away? Just delete it. Nailed the shot? Favorite it now, rather than hunt through your camera roll later.

We shipped our first update three days after the Duo's launch, and then listened to user feedback. Some users found the reviewer distracting, so we shipped a quick update that let you hide it. We also ran into more edge cases in the UI, such as needing to flip the toolbar from right to left in its split-app mode. That brings us to our second major update.

In today's update, we've found the perspective spot for the histogram: the crease. It's a bit of a "no man's land" for interaction when half-open, which makes it a good spot for auxiliary information.

When you hide the reviewer, we show our "XL" mode, maximizing the viewfinder to make the most of the big screen.

Lens controls move to the left, and it feels great to adjust focus with one hand while your other keeps your finger on the shutter button, just like a standalone camera.

Finally, we've added modes to the outer screen when fully open. You can mirror the camera view, which is great if you need to take a selfie with the best camera. Alternately, you can display a preview-only to avoid the distraction of controls.

We've also added an option to use the outer-screen as a softer alternative to the flash. Consider this shot.

Let's say I want to lift my face out of shadow, which is the job of a flash-fill. Unfortunately, the tiny flash on an iPhone is not great in this situation, unless you're going for a vintage Y2K look.

A larger light source, like the outer screen, yields more natural results even if it lacks the same power.

This is not going to work miracles, but if your subject is fairly close to the screen, you'll find that it provides softer, more even lighting.

Today's Halide Duo update is available now for all Mark III users.

I love the Duo. I'll find the tradeoffs worthwhile if I can be a little more productive on my phone. However, as someone who builds camera apps for a living, I'm far from giving up my iPhone Pro. Stay tuned for our 18 Pro review.

title: ★ Jon McCormack Retires From Apple
summary: Mark Gurman, reporting for Bloomberg today (gift link): Jon McCormack retired at the end of October after more than eight years at the company, according to people with knowledge of the matter. He oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how users capture, view and edit their pictures and video. Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to take over McCormack’s exact role. Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under another executive
reason: Gruber on the retirement of the executive behind iPhone Camera and Photos, a notable Apple leadership change.
content_html:
Mark Gurman, reporting for Bloomberg today (gift link):

Jon McCormack retired at the end of October after more than eight years at the company, according to people with knowledge of the matter. He oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying technology that determines how users capture, view and edit their pictures and video.

Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to take over McCormack’s exact role. Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under another executive, said the people, who asked not to be identified while discussing internal moves. An Apple spokesperson declined to comment.

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year.

I’ve met McCormack a few times. He frequently led media briefings for new iPhone camera features. He was always thoughtful, insightful, and fair. Like, sometimes his demonstrations would involve comparisons between photos of the same subjects and scenes captured on iPhones and ones captured with flagship Android phones. The photos were all good. It was never “Here are some beautiful images captured on iPhones and some dogshit ones from a Samsung and OnePlus”. The differences were often subtle. He’d even make the case for why someone might prefer the Android ones. But he could explain why Apple — and he personally — preferred the ones from the iPhone. Not just how the iPhone camera captures and processes images, but why. He also knew when to let the images speak for themselves.

McCormack was deeply informed at a technical level. He reported directly to Craig Federighi and that level of engineering acumen showed. I can’t recall any question being too technical for him to have a ready answer. One of the best iPhone camera innovations in recent years is the redesigned Center Stage selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 (and Air) lineup last year. The square sensor is hardware, and McCormack was a software VP, but the feature exemplifies the way hardware and software are developed in tandem at Apple. McCormack was the public face for that feature — and internally, pushed to make it happen. That square sensor is bigger, which means (a) it’s more expensive; and (b) it takes up more space internally. Both of those require winning hard-fought arguments inside Apple in order to ship. The bottom line is that it helps iPhone users take better photos of themselves — and according to McCormack himself, over 1 billion selfies are taken with iPhones every day. The influence Apple’s Camera team has on the daily lives of billions of people is significant; McCormack understood that.

But what really struck me about McCormack, right from the start, is that he is clearly a serious photographer himself. That’s perhaps understating it. He recently published a book of his own nature and travel photography: Patterns: Art of the Natural World. He discussed the book in an hour-long interview with his Apple colleague Pamela Chen, whose job title is one of the coolest I’ve ever heard: Chief Aesthetics Scientist. (Chen, unsurprisingly, is also a talented photographer.)

Gurman:

His departure comes at a time when Apple is navigating a fundamental shift in photography. Competitors such as Alphabet Inc.’s Google and Samsung Electronics Co. have increasingly embraced generative AI features that allow users to make substantial changes to images. That has blurred the distinction between capturing a real moment and creating an artificial one.

Two years ago in his iPhone 16 Pro review, returning to his repeated theme of “What is a photo?”, Nilay Patel quoted, at length, the answer he got from McCormack. I, in turn, quoted Patel quoting McCormack, and added:

McCormack’s response is genuinely thoughtful, and resonates deeply with my own personal take. But it’s worth noting that Apple is the conservative company when it comes to generative AI and photography — and yet they’re still shipping Clean Up. I’m not complaining about Clean Up’s existence. I’ve already used it personally. I’m just saying that even Apple’s stance involves significant use of generative AI.

This year, Apple added “extend” and “reframe” alongside Clean Up. I don’t love either of those features simply because I don’t like how they change the meaning of “What is a photo?”, but I don’t hate them either. We can’t put the generative AI genie back in the bottle. Apple, still, is the conservative company in the generative AI phone photography space.

Jon McCormack had a knack for shepherding good new features into the Camera app. But also, based on conversations I’ve had with multiple people who worked with him at Apple, McCormack was great at keeping stupid ideas out of the Camera app. Good new features that ship get more recognition than stupid new features that never ship — but the latter, I would argue, is the rarer and more important management skill. It’s far more important to keep stupid ideas out of any app than it is to add good new features. McCormack was the protector of the Camera app. Under his leadership, it remains focused on the craft and art of photography.

Lastly, everyone I know who worked with him loves the guy. McCormack was the perfect guy for an essential job, and he leaves big shoes to fill.

title: PHP: Mixed-Case URL Schemes Can Expose Data
summary: PHP (Mattias Geniar): PHP’s HTTP and FTP stream wrappers can send data without encryption when an HTTPS or FTPS URL has an uppercase S in its scheme, for example HTTPS://, httpS:// or FTPS://. Applications using file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions may therefore expose passwords, authentication tokens, request bodies or transferred files to an attacker […]
reason: A subtle real-world transport security bug where an uppercase S silently drops TLS in PHP streams.
content_html:
PHP (Mattias Geniar):

PHP’s HTTP and FTP stream wrappers can send data without encryption when an HTTPS or FTPS URL has an uppercase S in its scheme, for example HTTPS://, httpS:// or FTPS://. Applications using file_get_contents(), fopen() or other stream functions may therefore expose passwords, authentication tokens, request bodies or transferred files to an attacker able to observe the network traffic.

[…]

Mixed-case URLs passed by an application have been affected since PHP 5.2.0, and redirects to a mixed-case URL since PHP 4.3.0.

That was in 2002. It’s now been fixed in PHP 8.5.13 and other versions.

There’s also a new PHP 8.6 (Hacker News). Lots of security fixes recently.

title: phpAfterShell Explained: How Hackers Could Turn a PHP Session Flaw Into Code Execution
summary: PHP's default file-based session storage can be made to return objects an attacker chose, by cutting off a session write at the right moment. When combined with a second weakness, such as a suitable gadget chain in the app, those objects can allow the attacker to run code on the server. Today's PHP releases fix the flaw, called phpAfterShell. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-126714 and rated
reason: A clear explainer of how a race in PHP session writes can be chained into remote code execution.
content_html:
PHP's default file-based session storage can be made to return objects an attacker chose, by cutting off a session write at the right moment. When combined with a second weakness, such as a suitable gadget chain in the app, those objects can allow the attacker to run code on the server.

Today's PHP releases fix the flaw, called phpAfterShell.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-126714 and rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 scale by PHP's maintainers. Depthfirst, a security company, says it found the flaw and reported it to the maintainers.

The October 21 PHP releases, which fixed two critical flaws known as PHP2Shell, do not contain this fix. Servers updated then remain affected until they install today's releases. Neither the maintainers nor the company reports any attacks using phpAfterShell.

Who Is Affected and What to Do

These releases are affected, according to the maintainers' security advisory:

Branch Affected releases Fixed release
PHP 8.2 Before 8.2.36 8.2.36
PHP 8.3 Before 8.3.37 8.3.37
PHP 8.4 Before 8.4.28 8.4.28
PHP 8.5 Before 8.5.13 8.5.13

PHP 8.6.0, also released today, includes the fix.

The flaw is in the files session handler, which PHP uses by default. Sessions kept in Redis, a database, or another store are outside this defect, though each store's handling of a cut-off update needs its own check.

Whether an attacker needs to log in depends on how the app exposes its session handling.

On the path the company tested, the attacker uses upload progress, a PHP feature that records the progress of a file upload in the user's session. Where the feature is on, a multipart form upload that carries its field makes PHP write to the session before the app's own code runs. The app does not need an upload page, only any page that opens the session later.

PHP 8.1 and older are end-of-life. The official end-of-life mitigation branches for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are not affected, but older unpatched builds of those versions are, according to the company.

The company's remediation guidance sets out these steps:

  • Install the fixed release for your branch, as listed above. If you run PHP 8.1 or older, move to a supported branch.
  • Rebuild any container images and redeploy.
  • Check that the PHP version serving web requests is the new one.

If you cannot update yet and your app does not use upload progress, set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the server's PHP settings, then restart the PHP workers. Also limit the untrusted data your app stores in sessions.

Switching the feature off is not a full fix. It closes the upload path, but apps that put attacker-controlled data into sessions in other ways remain affected, the maintainers say.

The maintainers listed the same setting on October 21 as a temporary measure for one of the PHP2Shell flaws. Servers that have kept it off since then still need the update.

Moving sessions to a store that replaces records in one step also avoids this defect. The update is still the recommended fix for sites that keep the files handler.

Linux distribution packages may include the fix without changing the PHP version number, according to the company, so the version number alone may not indicate whether a server is fixed.

Once installed, the fixed releases empty the session file before each write and stop the write if that step fails. A cut-off write can still lose session data, but it can no longer leave old data behind for an attacker to use.

The updates also switch upload progress off by default. The Hacker News compared PHP's source code for the October 21 releases and today's. The built-in setting is on in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and off in 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6.0.

The release notes do not mention or explain the change. The sample php.ini files still show the old setting in a commented-out line. A php.ini file, distribution package, or hosting panel that switches the setting on will keep it on.

Where nothing else sets it, apps that rely on upload progress will need it switched back on after the update.

The same releases also fix other PHP security flaws.

How the Attack Works

The attack starts with the session write that upload progress makes before the app's code runs, Depthfirst's researchers say in their technical analysis.

A PHP session file stores each value as a name followed by serialized data. Length fields in that data tell PHP where each string ends, and nothing in the file marks a write as finished.

PHP locks the file while it writes, but the lock cannot undo a write that stops halfway. If the worker process dies partway through, the file can retain the start of the new data and the end of the old data.

By setting the lengths in the new data, an attacker can make text that sat harmlessly inside the old data read as a separate record, including a serialized object. The next request that calls session_start() loads that record and creates the object.

The researchers' public proof uses a harmless built-in object, stdClass, which appears in the session once the file is mixed.

The emergency PHP2Shell fixes on October 21 addressed an earlier attack via the same step.

"The original exploit stopped working, but the underlying problem was still there," the researchers say of the PHP2Shell patch.

That exploit needed objects to become active while PHP recorded upload progress, so the maintainers limited which classes can load at that moment. The change did not touch the file write. The object data still reaches the disk and becomes active later, when an ordinary request calls session_start().

The attack depends on stopping the write at the right moment. The maintainers say one way is a hard memory-limit failure in another thread of a threaded PHP build, which can kill the process mid-write.

Code execution then still needs a suitable gadget chain in the app, and the flaw can also corrupt session state.

In the researchers' own Linux tests, PHP's execution timeout fired only after the write had finished, so they used an out-of-memory kill to stop the worker mid-write instead.

The planted object appeared on the 11th attempt in a fresh run. That count measures getting the file into the right state on their servers, not how often code execution succeeds.

Their own chain needed no gadget from the app, the researchers say. It used a second bug instead, memory corruption in one of PHP's built-in classes.

They are holding back its details for coordinated disclosure and have not said whether that bug is fixed in today's releases.

The same trick can also replace ordinary session values, such as who is logged in, their permissions, or a CSRF token, before the app checks them, the researchers say.

Google News,

reason: A former CISO unpacks the FBI ARTEX advisory and how attackers reach privileged access in hours.
content_html:
Gone in three hours: What ARTEX does with your credentials

Threat actors can now go from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. Your change advisory board takes longer to approve a firewall rule.

That figure comes from the FBI’s November 13 advisory, FBI FLASH-20261113-001, about a framework called ARTEX. The read as a recovering CISO: all the techniques in the alert are familiar, but the clock has changed. Every credential you left lying around just got easier to pick up.

What is ARTEX, and how does it automate cyberattacks?

ARTEX is an open-source, multi-agent pentesting framework written in Go. An operator types in an objective in plain language. LLM-backed agents turn it into commands, load the proper scripts, and run them.

The developer published it on GitHub in July 2026 for authorized testing. The FBI reports malicious use since at least August. A month from the initial release to abuse is, for an offensive security tool.

After reports of misuse surfaced, the developer pulled the repository on October 8. But, forks, mirrors, archives, and a commercial version keep it in circulation because the internet has never once given anything back. The Internet never forgets. By early November, researchers counted more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles.

The reported targets span at least ten market segments worldwide, including financial services, government, healthcare, and energy. One financially motivated campaign exfiltrated personal information on about 67,000 people. In another incident, a supply chain compromise at a cloud backup service opened access to more than 2,250 downstream tenants.

Where does ARTEX find credentials?

The alert maps the activity to 43 ATT&CK techniques. Read it by phase and one thing keeps turning up: a credential somebody forgot about.

  • Reconnaissance. Agents tested the permissions of Azure credentials, including SAS tokens, service principals, Kudu credentials, and storage account keys, with sub-second checks.

  • Initial access. Hardcoded administrator passwords in JavaScript bundles, weak administrative credentials, compromised vendor credentials through trusted B2B federation, and stolen VPN configurations with leaked credentials.

  • Persistence. Account takeover through password resets, new SSH key pairs, and credentials added to existing OAuth applications.

  • Privilege escalation. Cloud compute instances launched with high-value IAM roles, harvested Kerberos Service Tickets, DCSync to steal the Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (KRBTGT) key, and an administrator token forged with unrotated authentication keys.

  • Internal reconnaissance. More than 110,000 Active Directory objects enumerated, and Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords read.

On paper, an admin password in a JavaScript bundle is T1552.001. In practice, it is a sticky note on the monitor, served from a CDN.

One piece of good news: endpoint protection blocked attempted lateral movement to domain controllers through Pass-the-Ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay, and Pass-the-Hash. So boring controls are still earning their keep.

Why do AI-driven attacks make exposed credentials more dangerous?

Automation changes the price of one exposed credential. A hardcoded password or an unrotated signing key used to wait for a human with time and motivation. Now an agent tests it in under a second and feeds the result into the next technique.

Two variables decide how quickly an exposed credential can become a broader incident:

  • Standing access sets how far the credential reaches once it is used

  • Detection time sets how long you have, and three hours is less than some incident bridges need to agree on a severity level

So we have stopped planning around a patient attacker. Assume anything discoverable gets discovered, and anything valid gets tried.

Five ways to reduce ARTEX-related credential exposure this week

The FBI's credential recommendations are specific. The controls below are theirs.

  1. Sweep for embedded secrets. Review application configurations, environment variables, infrastructure-as-code, deployment scripts, and CI/CD pipelines. I would add shipped front-end bundles, since that is where the alert found admin passwords.

  2. Rotate what you find, promptly. Include signing and authentication keys. The forged admin token in the alert relied on keys nobody had rotated.

  3. Restrict deployment and publishing credentials. List every person and pipeline that can read them today. Cut the list to the ones that deploy.

  4. Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants. Revoke what nobody uses.

  5. Monitor credential additions and privileged role assignments. Monitor the speed of identity access, and spikes in API traffic.

Steps one and two fit in a week for most teams. Steps three to five need a named owner and a date, or they become a slide.

Where 1Password helps reduce credential exposure

Several 1Password capabilities are aligned with those recommendations. The FBI does not endorse products, and each capability has a boundary you should know before you count on it.

  • Developer Watchtower, in the 1Password desktop apps for Mac, Windows, and Linux, finds unencrypted or insecure SSH keys in ~/.ssh and .env files with plaintext secrets in nine named development folders. It only checks files on local disk that match .env naming patterns, so it doesn’t look at remote repositories or Git history, and other file types like a JavaScript bundle are outside its view even when they sit in a scanned folder..

  • Privileged Access provides just-in-time, task-scoped access to cloud environments with automatic deprovisioning, and discovers overprivileged cloud identities. It applies only to access granted through Privileged Access.

  • SaaS Manager finds apps with high-risk OAuth scopes and revokes their tokens in Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID.

  • 1Password Developer Tools, allow for JIT secret injection to coding agents and CI/CD pipelines including GitHub Actions, validates the workload identity against registered policy and releases only the secrets that are scoped to the task only for the duration of the workflow. Secrets are available to the job during the run. They are not single-use or bound to a runner.

None of this is a claim about the ARTEX intrusions themselves. A vendor telling you its product would have stopped a breach it was not present for should make you check your wallet.

What credential hygiene will not fix

Most of the ARTEX activity sits outside credential management: web application exploitation, Kerberos attacks, web shells, and command and control. The FBI's guidance also covers reducing the external attack surface, strengthening application protections, and preserving evidence for response. A vault does nothing for an unpatched web app.

The facts here reflect the FLASH as published on November 13, 2026. They may change as investigations continue.

Two actions to take before Today

  1. Read FBI FLASH-20261113-001 and send the mitigations section to the person responsible for your CI/CD pipelines

  2. Search your production JavaScript bundles for the string "password." A hit is your first rotation ticket and your opening story at the next all-hands

title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
summary: Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That's according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant. […]
reason: Apple is staffing up to build an agent that uses apps and writes code, a big shift in its AI strategy.
content_html:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent

Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

content_html:
Examine the climatological precipitation map for Washington State, and the heaviest precipitation is on the western slopes of the Cascades and Olympic Mountains (see below)

This is expected because most of our precipitation comes from moist air moving eastward off the Pacific.  Air that is forced to rise, cool, and precipitate on the west-facing major slopes of our region.

But something VERY different occurred during the 36 hours ending Thursday evening (see below).  The heaviest precipitation was on the EASTERN slopes of the Cascades and the southeastern slopes of the Olympics (see below)

Very little on the western slopes of the Cascades.


The visible satellite image on Thursday morning shows clouds east of the Cascade crest. Nearly clear on the western side.


Substantial snow fell on the eastern slopes of the Cascades, as shown by an image provided by the NW Avalanche Center for a location just east of Stevens Pass.   I am tempted to get out my skis!




Even as far west as Crystal Mountain, a fresh cover of the white stuff was apparent.


Want to be really impressed with the changes?  Below is the change in snowpack during the past three days.   Massive increase in snow east of the Cascade crest of Oregon and Washington.


The UW WRF modeling system predicted this east-side precipitation (see below) days before (see below).


It also forecast the eastern slopes getting snow (see below).


So why the precipitation reversal?

Easy to explain.  

A low center passed south of us, pushing moisture north into eastern Washington, and then swinging the moisture toward the west on the eastern slopes of the Cascades.   

This is illustrated by the 850 hPa (about 5000 ft) and 500 hPa (about 18,000 ft) maps below for 4 PM Wednesday (below).  You can see the easterly (from the east) winds approaching the Cascades.

850 hPa pressure, 5000 ft


500 hPa 18,000 ft

This pattern, with lows going into our south, has occurred several times during the last few weeks, but the latest forecasts suggest a substantial pattern shift with precipitation falling preferentially on the western slopes during the next week or so.



Looking east from the Cascades crest.

title: Get rid of Siri AI’s aggressive writing controls in Mail
summary: There I was, drafting an email reply in macOS 27.2.1, when I was greeted by this fresh hell: I’ve been on record since the 27 releases as saying that I find Siri’s writing tools across the platform updates to be unnecessarily aggressive, and they certainly haven’t gotten less so.…
reason: Six Colors on Siri AI writing controls in Mail, a favorite writer on timely Apple news.
content_html:
There I was, drafting an email reply in macOS 27.2.1, when I was greeted by this fresh hell:

I’ve been on record since the 27 releases as saying that I find Siri’s writing tools across the platform updates to be unnecessarily aggressive, and they certainly haven’t gotten less so.

Look, I’m a professional writer. I do not need help writing a three-sentence email. If there are people who find these features useful, have at! But I would love the ability to dispatch them with extreme prejudice, and I can find no options anywhere in Mail to say “begone with you!”

But all hope is not lost. After complaining on Mastodon1, Andrew Kemp offered this suggestion:

Lo and behold, yes! If you open up System Settings and go to Screen Time > Content & Privacy, then turn on the Content & Privacy switch, you can then go into the Siri sub-menu and turn off Writing Assistance. (You can also disable other Siri options in here, such as Broad World Knowledge, Image Creation, and Realistic Images, all of which probably make more sense for the parental controls for which Screen Time is designed.)

I had to close and re-open my draft message, but when I did, it was back to just the formatting bar. Phew.

I don’t love having to turn to Screen Time for this feature any more than I like the idea of using accessibility features for aesthetic alterations to the OS, but any port in a storm, I suppose.

I know we’re in the era of “shove AI into everything!” but I have generally appreciated Apple’s more conservative stance here. I just wish they would give us more granular options for turning off the parts of these features we don’t want that doesn’t require parenting ourselves.

  1. Something I’m all too capable of doing, even on paternity leave. ↩

title: Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts
summary: A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean. On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled. Fixed kernels shipped
reason: KVM flaw exposing host memory from a guest VM matters for cloud security and confidential computing.
content_html:
A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years.

In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities.

What to Do

The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted.

Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range.

Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected.

Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change.

Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it:

  • Check the setting with 
    cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested
    . A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on.
  • If the host cannot be updated yet, add 
    options kvm_amd nested=0
    to the host's module configuration.
  • Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with 
    uname -r
    and by reading the nested setting again.

The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

title: Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own
summary: Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full […]
reason: AI agents autonomously finding a zero-day is a notable security and AI shift.
content_html:
Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

Discovery

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

Cairn and an overview of this campaign

Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. The following operations show both the persistence and the capability of autonomous AI agents.

Persistence against a hardened target

The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.

When those attempts failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded.

A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login.

Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction.

Zero-day discovery

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

Subsequent use

In another session, the threat actor stepped in. After the agents discovered the zero-day, the actor then provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network. The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel. The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.

Attribution

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor based on the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time script timestamps, and the targeting of universities likely of strategic interest to China.

Actions taken by AWS

Amazon Threat Intelligence notified the project’s maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory.

The affected organizations were non-AWS customers that AWS had no direct path to notify. Instead, AWS worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.

Adoption is growing

Gambit Security was one of the first organizations in the industry to document the use of Cairn by a threat group. Its research describes a separate, financially motivated actor using Cairn to target online retailers. Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations. Additional details are available in Gambit Security’s report.

What this means for defenders

The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints. To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.

Behind the scenes, AWS active defense systems use global honeypots (decoy systems that attract threat actors) and network traffic analysis to identify actors that are scanning for vulnerable systems, and then help restrict that activity at the network level. These protections are built into the AWS network at no extra cost to customers.

Indicators of compromise

The following addresses appear in records dated September 8 to 10, 2026.

142[.]4.98.145

142[.]4.107.34

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

CJ Moses

CJ Moses is the CISO of Amazon Integrated Security. In his role, CJ leads security engineering and operations across Amazon. His mission is to enable Amazon businesses by making the benefits of security the path of least resistance. CJ joined Amazon in December 2007, holding various roles including Consumer CISO, and most recently AWS CISO, before becoming CISO of Amazon Integrated Security September of 2023.

Prior to joining Amazon, CJ led the technical analysis of computer and network intrusion efforts at the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Cyber Division. CJ also served as a Special Agent with the Air Force Office of Special Investigations (AFOSI). CJ led several computer intrusion investigations seen as foundational to the security industry today.

CJ holds degrees in Computer Science and Criminal Justice, and is an active SRO GT America GT2 race car driver.

title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
summary: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users' messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are "undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy," Signal president […]
reason: Signal blocking AI agents from reading the screen touches security and AI agents.
content_html:
Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.

Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen

Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”

Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system.

Signal’s app security settings on Android devices will display this message for the screenshot-blocking feature.

Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

title: China-Linked Hackers Exploit Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day to Gain Admin Access and Steal Data
summary: The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized
reason: VMware vCenter zero-day exploited by a China-linked group, a notable breach.
content_html:
The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system.

It has been addressed as part of patches released on November 19, 2026, in the following versions -

  • VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.1.0200
  • VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0200
  • VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m
  • VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)
  • VMware Cloud Foundation - Fixed in 5.2.5
  • VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)
  • VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

"CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC)," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said.

"Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local."

An attacker can exploit the vulnerability to obtain an authenticated administrator session, execute arbitrary commands, and acquire files, such as the data.mdb database, by using the Directory Service ("vmdird"). The tech giant's threat intelligence and incident response teams said it observed the Chinese hacking group weaponizing the flaw using a utility dubbed BONESAW.

"BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang, which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account," Google said.

The activity is part of the same campaign that also involved the exploitation of a then zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to conduct reconnaissance, obtain administrative control, establish persistence, and deploy a bespoke proxy tunneler called BARECLAW.

From the Remote Support device, the threat actor is said to have moved laterally to an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and deployed additional payloads to broaden their access, map the environment, conduct data theft, and move into the virtualized environment.

"The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012," Google said. "Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of Armory Castle's remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW."

Deployed as part of the attack are six identified malware families and utilities -

  • SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, JSP web shells designed to run arbitrary commands, stage payloads, and establish a foothold on the Linux appliance.
  • BONESAW, the Golang-based remote exploitation utility for CVE-2026-123890 used to target an internal vCenter Server.
  • SAWSNAKE, a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, thereby making it possible to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW and allowing the attacker to forge authentication tokens, bypass multi-factor authentication(MFA), and impersonate any user. It's a Go-based port of an open-source Python script named "vcenter_saml_login.py."
  • BEARBONES, a C backdoor based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server that's capable of bypassing system password authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from the temporary directory.
  • LAZYBONES, a lightweight Go backdoor that uses Slack for command-and-control (C2) communications and has been previously deployed in a separate intrusion in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of a critical flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2025-22457, CVSS score: 9.0).

It's suspected that Armory Castle had knowledge of the flaw prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026, with the recovered BONESAW binary containing a build timestamp of July 13, 2026. However, it's worth noting that build metadata can be modified before compilation.

"After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, Armory Castle moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-<REDACTED>@vsphere.local," Google said.

"Notably, Armory Castle enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. After enabling SSH, Armory Castle connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account."

In the final stage of the attack, the adversary was found enumerating the ESXi file system, mounting Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and adding an SSH public key to the root account's authorized keys. It also conducted additional reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi file system, which were then archived and downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance for subsequent exfiltration.

Furthermore, the attackers have been observed dropping LAZYBONES to a separate Linux appliance, which periodically checks for commands from a designated Slack channel, allowing it to perform command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment.

CVE-2026-123890 is the second vulnerability in a VMware product to be exploited by Armory Castle as a zero-day this year alone. Late last month, CrowdStrike revealed it identified incidents where the hacking crew abused CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an insufficient logging flaw in VMware ESX, to reduce audit trail visibility.

"BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days," Google said. "The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each."

"The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting Armory Castle operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor's operational commitment to compromise high-priority targets."

Google News,

title: New Unpatched Windows 0-Day FastUnlock Lets Someone Holding a Locked PC Run Programs on It
summary: A newly disclosed unpatched zero-day technique called FastUnlock lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows computer start programs without signing in. Whoever uses it gets only a limited account, not administrator control of the machine. The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker
reason: Unpatched Windows lock-screen bypass is relevant to a Microsoft security PM.
content_html:
A newly disclosed unpatched zero-day technique called FastUnlock lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows computer start programs without signing in. Whoever uses it gets only a limited account, not administrator control of the machine.

The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker tested it the same day and found it works.

There is no fix from Microsoft yet, and nothing shows the method has been used in a real attack.

The technique does not work on every machine. It requires physical access to the computer and a Microsoft account accessible through the lock screen's recovery options, and it uses Windows' built-in screen reader, Narrator, to navigate the locked screen.

In its test, the firm reached a point where it could run a program from the lock screen in a limited account that ThreatLocker identified as WSIAccount and said is "not an administrator account."

The researcher's GitHub disclosure is a short post with a video and little written detail, so the clearest account of what the flaw does comes from the firm's independent test.

Many Windows computers encrypt their drives with BitLocker, but in a common setup, that does not make them immune to this technique. A chip called the TPM unlocks the drive automatically when the computer starts, so by the time the lock screen appears, the files are already readable, and the bypass runs at that point. Microsoft's own TPM documentation describes this mode, in which the drive unlocks "without having to enter a PIN."

FastUnlock does not break that encryption or recover the key. It runs on a computer that has already unlocked its own drive in the normal way, which is a smaller problem than cracking an encrypted disk, though still a real one for a machine someone else is holding.

The conditions above, physical access and a reachable Microsoft account, are what put a machine at risk. No official list of affected Windows versions has been published, so treat any machine that meets those conditions as possibly affected until one is.

What You Can Do Now

With no patch available, the useful steps are about physical control and startup protection.

  • Keep machines that can go missing out of the wrong hands. Lock away or closely manage laptops, shared desks, and front-counter computers that a stranger could reach.
  • On sensitive machines, add a startup PIN to BitLocker instead of letting the drive unlock on its own.
  • Shut down or hibernate devices when they leave someone's control. A startup PIN protects only a machine that has not yet started, not one already on the lock screen.
  • Do not treat a locked screen on its own as enough.

Microsoft's countermeasures guidance recommends using a startup PIN, along with shutting down or hibernating machines when faced with determined, hands-on attackers. Until an official fix or advisory appears, watch for one and apply it when it comes.

reason: Apple can finally confirm the UK backdoor demand behind pulling Advanced Data Protection, a landmark encryption policy story.
content_html:
Apple can at last admit what everyone knew about its restriction in February 2025 on iCloud’s Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for new users in the United Kingdom: the government made us do it.

ADP provides end-to-end, device-based encryption for most iCloud data, and it was a remarkable bump up in privacy protection when Apple released it suddenly in December 2022. The February 2025 announcement offered no details as to why Apple made this enrollment change.

Reporting in April 2025 revealed that the UK government had demanded Apple build a backdoor for access to iCloud data under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which also prevented Apple from revealing this demand. Apple instead disabled the feature for new users.

On Thursday, the UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent body that allows challenges to government surveillance orders, said—paraphrasing—it was ridiculous for Apple to be unable to discuss something widely known in public.

Apple challenged an original broad order that would have jeopardized privacy for users worldwide, and a second one that more narrowly set the scope for British citizens. The company told some media outlets that it “welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.”
