title: Scope down permissions of existing sessions using AWS STS GetScopedCredentials
summary: When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it. GetScopedCredentials is a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that you can use to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security […]
reason: New STS API to scope down session credentials for AI agents, a least-privilege pattern relevant to agent security.
content_html:
When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it. GetScopedCredentials is a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that you can use to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security credentials. You can assign each agent, sub-agent, or process its own set of credentials that keep the caller’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity but carry reduced permissions, a shorter session duration, or both.

You can call GetScopedCredentials with the temporary security credentials you already use, such as those from aws login, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance profile, or an AWS Lambda function. In each call, you pass a scope down policy, a shorter session duration, or both. A scope down policy is an inline policy that describes the maximum permissions for the new credentials. The resulting permissions are the intersection of your session’s effective permissions and the scope down policy, so they can only be reduced. Similarly, the session duration you request can’t exceed the remaining duration of the calling session. You can also call GetScopedCredentials again with the resulting credentials to scope down permissions or reduce session duration even further.

GetScopedCredentials is designed as a building block. Because it scopes down permissions on the credentials you already have, you can build it into agent frameworks, services that issue credentials to other components, continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, and your own applications. You can also call it again with scoped-down credentials, so an orchestrating agent can give each sub-agent narrower access than its own.

In this post, we walk through a few common use cases to get you started, show you how to call GetScopedCredentials, and explain how to manage access to it.

Example use cases

You can use GetScopedCredentials whenever a workload needs narrower access than the session that starts it. Examples include limiting what AI agents can do, scoping down permissions based on runtime context, and granting just-in-time access. We cover two of the most common use cases in more detail in this section.

Limit what AI agents can do

When you pass credentials to an agent, the agent can use any permission those credentials carry. An agent decides which actions to take at runtime, often based on prompts or tool output. If its credentials are overly permissive, an agent that makes a mistake can act beyond the task you gave it.

Before you pass credentials to an agent, you can use GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions to only what its tasks require, such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. You could also take the opposite approach and keep most of its permissions while removing only the actions the agent should never perform, such as deleting resources. An orchestrating agent can do the same for each sub-agent it starts. Because a scope down operation can only narrow permissions, a sub-agent never has more access than the agent that started it. To help ensure that your agents only have access to the scoped-down credentials, run them in isolated or sandbox environments such as AWS Strands Box.

Scope down permissions based on runtime context

Many workloads run under a single IAM role but need different, narrower permissions for each task they perform. The right set of permissions for a task often depends on information the workload learns only at runtime, such as who sent a request.

Consider a multi-tenant application that stores each tenant’s files under a separate prefix in one S3 bucket. This application uses a single IAM role to serve all its tenants, so the role can access every tenant’s prefix. However, each request should reach only the files of the tenant who sent it, and the application learns which tenant that is only after it authenticates the request. At that point, a trusted credential broker in the application takes the tenant details from the authenticated session and calls GetScopedCredentials with a scope down policy that allows access only to that tenant’s prefix. It passes only the scoped-down credentials to the worker that handles the request, so Amazon S3 denies that worker access to other tenants’ prefixes even though the original role covers them all.

How to call GetScopedCredentials

This section walks through the process of scoping down permissions for an existing session. Before you call GetScopedCredentials, make sure you have valid temporary security credentials and that they have the permissions to call the API. The following identity based policy grants that permission.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "sts:GetScopedCredentials",
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}

To call GetScopedCredentials, use the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language.

Step 1: Define a scope down policy

Write a scope down policy that describes the maximum permissions the resulting credentials should have. At launch, GetScopedCredentials accepts one inline scope down policy of up to 2,048 characters. You can write a scope down policy in many ways, such as authoring a policy from scratch, reusing or modifying an existing policy, or asking an AI assistant to draft one. This section covers two such approaches.

Option A: Write the policy yourself

If you know which actions and resources your task needs, write the policy directly. The following sample policy allows the resulting credentials to only read objects from a single S3 bucket.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"
  }]
}

Make sure to include every action the task needs, including dependent actions. For example, if your task uses Amazon Athena to query data in Amazon S3, the policy must also allow s3:GetObject on that data, because Athena reads it with your credentials.

To keep most of the calling session’s permissions and remove only a few sensitive ones, use an Allow statement with NotAction. This statement doesn’t grant additional access, because a scope down policy can only reduce permissions. The resulting credentials keep the calling session’s permissions except the actions you list, which makes this a quick way to set guardrails without listing each action a task needs. The following sample policy blocks identity and account management, assuming other roles, and deleting some critical resources.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "NotAction": [
      "iam:*",
      "organizations:*",
      "account:*",
      "sts:AssumeRole*",
      "s3:DeleteBucket",
      "ec2:TerminateInstances",
      "rds:DeleteDBInstance",
      "dynamodb:DeleteTable"
    ],
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}

Option B: Generate the policy with IAM Policy Autopilot

You can also use IAM Policy Autopilot to generate a scope down policy. IAM Policy Autopilot is an open source tool from AWS that analyzes the AWS SDK calls in your code and identifies the permissions it requires to run successfully. You can run it from the command line or as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in your AI coding assistant. To install it, see the Getting Started instructions for IAM Policy Autopilot.

We’ll use the following Python code to generate a scope down policy using IAM Policy Autopilot. It records a report’s status in an Amazon DynamoDB table.

import json
import logging
import os

import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb")
table_name = os.environ["TABLE_NAME"]


def _response(status_code, message):
    return {"statusCode": status_code, "body": json.dumps({"message": message})}


def handler(event, context):
    try:
        request = json.loads(event.get("body") or "{}")
        report_id = request["reportId"]
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError):
        return _response(400, "Request body must be JSON with a reportId")

    if not isinstance(report_id, str) or not report_id:
        return _response(400, "reportId must be a non-empty string")

    try:
        dynamodb.put_item(
            TableName=table_name,
            Item={
                "reportId": {"S": report_id},
                "status": {"S": "READY"},
            },
            ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(reportId)",
        )
        return _response(200, "Report status saved")
    except ClientError as error:
        code = error.response["Error"]["Code"]
        if code == "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
            return _response(409, "Report status already exists")

        logger.error("PutItem failed: %s", code)
        return _response(500, "Unable to save the report status")

Save the code as report_status.py and run the following command. If the generated policy exceeds the 2,048 character limit, set the max-policy-size and allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size options to 2048. IAM Policy Autopilot then replaces groups of actions with wildcards to fit that size and warns you if it can’t.

iam-policy-autopilot generate-policies ./report_status.py \
  --region us-west-2 \
  --account 123456789012 \
  --service-hints dynamodb \
  --max-policy-size 2048 \
  --allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size 2048 \
  --pretty

IAM Policy Autopilot returns the following policy.

{
  "Id": "IamPolicyAutopilot",
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "dynamodb:PutItem",
        "dynamodb:WriteDataForReplication"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/*"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:ViaService": [
            "dynamodb.us-west-2.amazonaws.com"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

IAM Policy Autopilot generates a starting policy that can include wildcards, either because specific resources can’t be inferred from the code, such as with the table/* and key/* resources in this example, or because an optional parameter that limits policy size replaced actions with wildcards. Review the generated policies and replace the wildcards with the actions and resources your task should access.

However you create the policy, save it as scope-down-policy.json. If you want to continue calling GetScopedCredentials with the resulting credentials, also include the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in the Allow block of the permission policy.

Step 2: Call GetScopedCredentials

Pass the scope down policy you created to GetScopedCredentials. The following command also uses the optional duration-seconds parameter to limit the resulting session duration and the optional scoped-session-description parameter to record context for the scoped-down credentials. If you omit the duration-seconds parameter, the credentials keep the calling session’s remaining duration.

aws sts get-scoped-credentials \
  --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"}]}' \
  --duration-seconds 300 \
  --scoped-session-description report-status-job \
  --region us-west-2

The response includes a new set of temporary security credentials, a SessionInfo element, and some helpful information about session size and contents.

{
  "Credentials": {
    "AccessKeyId": "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE",
    "SecretAccessKey": "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY,
    "SessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...",
    "Expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z"
  },
  "SessionInfo": {
    "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane",
    "ScopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane"
  },
  "SessionTokenUtilization": 17,
  "SessionTokenSize": 724,
  "ScopedPoliciesCount": 1
}

Notice that the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the SessionInfo element matches the ARN of your calling session. The scoped-down credentials retain the identity of the calling session, including the role session name, session tags and context keys.

The ScopedPoliciesCount value in the response shows how many scope down policies apply to the session. It increases only when a recursive call adds a new scope down policy and not when a call only shortens the session duration.

Each GetScopedCredentials call is logged in AWS CloudTrail. The following event, shortened for readability, shows the call from this example.

{
    "eventVersion": "1.11",
    "userIdentity": {

The scopedSessionDescription value in the CloudTrail event records the text you passed to the API call earlier. Later calls made with the scoped-down credentials show the scoped down session’s access key ID in userIdentity.accessKeyId, which can be used to trace back to its immediate parent session.

Step 3 (optional): Scope down the credentials again

You can call GetScopedCredentials recursively with the scoped-down credentials to narrow permissions or reduce session duration even further. You can apply a maximum of three scope down policies to a session, and each new scope down policy intersects with all prior ones. Recursive calls that only shorten the session duration and don’t add a scope down policy don’t count toward this limit. For a recursive call to succeed, every earlier scope down policy must allow the sts:GetScopedCredentials action.

Managing access to GetScopedCredentials

You can control access to the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in all relevant policy types. You can also use the sts:DurationSeconds condition key to limit the session duration of scoped-down credentials, and global condition keys such as aws:PrincipalArn, aws:PrincipalTag, and aws:SourceVpce to restrict who can call the API and from where.

Availability and request quota

GetScopedCredentials is available in all AWS commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. The API has a dedicated request quota of 200 requests per second per account in each Region at launch. You can use scoped-down credentials with most AWS services. For a list of services that aren’t supported, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference.

Conclusion

GetScopedCredentials gives you a building block for reducing permissions at runtime. This is particularly helpful when you want to give each agent, sub agent or workload only the access it needs.

For more information about GetScopedCredentials, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference. To learn how permissions are evaluated for scoped-down credentials, see Permissions for GetScopedCredentials and Policy evaluation for requests within a single account. Now go build!

title: Siri Recap Hands-On: Private, But Not Very Useful
summary: With the watchOS 27.3 beta , Apple started testing Siri Recap. ‌Siri‌ Recap lets the Series 12 and Ultra 4 Apple Watch models listen to conversations to generate a brief summary of what was discussed. Actual audio is sectioned off from apps, Apple, and the rest of the OS, and then discarded after a summary is generated. It's a privacy-forward way of tracking what's going on around you, but after two weeks of testing, it's clear that the privacy safeguards limit its usefulness. Overly brief summa
feed: MacRumors: Mac News and Rumors - All Stories
reason: Hands-on with Siri Recap, Apple's privacy-isolated conversation summaries on Apple Watch.
content_html:
With the watchOS 27.3 beta, Apple started testing Siri Recap. ‌Siri‌ Recap lets the Series 12 and Ultra 4 Apple Watch models listen to conversations to generate a brief summary of what was discussed. Actual audio is sectioned off from apps, Apple, and the rest of the OS, and then discarded after a summary is generated.


It's a privacy-forward way of tracking what's going on around you, but after two weeks of testing, it's clear that the privacy safeguards limit its usefulness. Overly brief summaries, lack of speaker labeling, and no original audio to compare against make ‌Siri‌ Recap unreliable.

Before I get into my experience, I want to make it clear that ‌Siri‌ Recap is a beta feature in beta software. It hasn't been released yet, Apple hasn't finished refining it, and it won't be available to the public until watchOS 27.3 launches in December. Still, the bones are in place. Some of the issues I encountered could improve before release, but others are the result of the way it's built.

My first recaps were from YouTube videos and Instagram Reels. ‌Siri‌ Recap can tell when I'm watching TV shows and movies, but it can't distinguish a YouTube video from a real-life conversation. I was surprised it summarized dialogue I wasn't involved in instead of waiting until it recognized my voice (which ‌Siri‌ can do). Listening in on ambient conversations makes it feel a little stalker-like. When ‌Siri‌ Recap is turned on, it's listening, and there's no indication for the people around you.


Most of my other recaps summarized short, inconsequential conversations with my partner that I don't need or want to revisit. I don't need to remember that my breakfast on Friday had one too many pieces of vegan bacon, or that my cat was playing with a silica packet. I don't need to remember discussions about Grand Theft Auto VI or that I saw a rabbit in the driveway the other day. There is an option to only have ‌Siri‌ Recap on at certain times of the day or in certain locations, which would eliminate that issue. Ironically, ‌Siri‌ did the best at summarizing shorter interactions I don't care about.


I've taken my cats to a few vet appointments recently, so I had an opportunity to test ‌Siri‌ Recap with genuinely important conversations where I get a flood of information. After the first visit, I learned ‌Siri‌ and I don't have the same opinion on the details that matter, and I found that summaries of longer conversations are just too concise and inaccurate to be helpful.

I told the vet my cat is picky and will only eat one kind of dry food, but stays hydrated because she drinks a lot of water. In a separate part of the conversation, I said she was gaining weight even though her prescription food isn't for kittens. ‌Siri‌ combined those two parts of the conversation into a summary that doesn't make sense, and I had that issue in almost every long conversation.

A few minutes later, I asked for a recommendation on heartworm medication because I've read about some problematic products that can make cats sick. The vet relayed a story about needing a particular brand for her cat because she has a rabbit at home, and rabbits are sensitive to a lot of medications. ‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't label speakers, so the summary of that conversation turned into a confusing amalgamation suggesting I have a rabbit at home. Inappropriately combining unrelated concepts is likely something that can be fixed, but the lack of speaker labels is intentional.


During a pre-surgery consultation, I think I ran into another limitation. Apple says potentially harmful content isn't summarized, which could cover a broad range of topics. Important parts of the conversation with the vet aren't in the summary, like some of the scarier surgical risks and resuscitation preferences. ‌Siri‌ doesn't say if anything was skipped because of the content, so I don't know if that information wasn't considered important or if it was filtered out.


Some of what ‌Siri‌ recapped was useful. If conversations were fact-heavy, ‌Siri‌ did a good job getting everything down, especially when dates were involved. I scheduled a follow-up appointment and ‌Siri‌ got the date right and the exact total of the bill when it was spoken aloud. Apple does say ‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't include financial info, so I'm not sure what counts. ‌Siri‌ is also surprisingly good at interpreting spoken medication names like benazepril and clopidogrel and correctly guessing what they're meant to be.


During a third vet visit, the recap did get many of the major points, but going over those notes made me realize this kind of summarization may not work, even when accurate. I had my own memory of the conversation and knew what I thought was important, but some of what ‌Siri‌ kept wasn't what mattered to me.

Those ‌Siri‌ details I re-read were cemented in my memory over other information when I revisited the conversation later in the week, subtly changing how I remember the appointment. I worry having notes that aren't my own will overwrite what I would have remembered without them. It's almost like having a picture of something that happened in my head, and then having someone tell me it happened differently.


‌Siri‌ Recap doesn't record full conversations for privacy reasons, but that leaves ‌Siri‌ to decide what to keep in a discussion and what's not. I don't trust ‌Siri‌ to make that kind of decision, personally. There's no option to go back and check what ‌Siri‌ left out since there are no recordings. I wouldn't want a version of ‌Siri‌ Recap that records full conversations because of the privacy concerns, but I'm not sure Apple has delivered a version that's both useful and privacy-forward.

‌Siri‌ picks and chooses what matters, and in my two-week test, ‌Siri‌ merged concepts and conversations in ways that were more confusing than helpful over and over again. ‌Siri‌ Recap isn't a feature I'm going to use, and it's not a feature I'd recommend to others.

title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
summary: President Donald Trump promised to put a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said at a […]
reason: A threatened tax on offshore AI data centers could reshape where cloud providers like Azure build.
content_html:
President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.

Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US

While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”

Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”

Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.

Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:

Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.

We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.

So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

title: Five Questions As BYU Fights Past Demons vs. Kansas
summary: BYU plays their final true road game of the regular season in Lawrence on Saturday. The Cougars and Jayhawks kick off at 10:00am MT on ESPN. We don’t need to remind BYU fans of the importance of this game or the demons that come to life when the Cougars play Kansas. 10th-ranked BYU’s College Football […]
reason: Preview of 10th ranked BYU's high-stakes road game at Kansas Saturday.
content_html:
BYU plays their final true road game of the regular season in Lawrence on Saturday. The Cougars and Jayhawks kick off at 10:00am MT on ESPN.

We don’t need to remind BYU fans of the importance of this game or the demons that come to life when the Cougars play Kansas. 10th-ranked BYU’s College Football Playoff hopes are very much alive. And they very much are at stake when these two teams square off at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium.

Let’s dive into five questions ahead of the matchup.

What demons are the Cougars facing against the Jayhawks?

For starters, BYU has never beaten Kansas in football in three tries. Somehow, the Cougars have had more success against Kansas in basketball than football. The matchup everyone seems to be pointing to is the one in 2024. It’s a very similar situation. The Jayhawks traveled to Provo in mid-November with BYU at 9-0 with College Football Playoff hopes very alive. Kansas came with an unremarkable 3-6 record but had just beaten a ranked Iowa State team. BYU turned the ball over twice and committed one of the worst special teams blunders imaginable. A punt in a short field by Kansas while BYU was up three bounced off Evan Johnson’s helmet. Kansas recovered the muff and scored a few plays later to take the lead. It was one of the most devastating losses in recent BYU history.

Before that, Kansas and BYU met up in 2023, the Cougars’ last trip to Lawrence before this weekend. After leading 17-14 at halftime, BYU allowed 24 second half points as they unraveled, losing what was their first official Big 12 Conference game.

The demons didn’t start there either. The first meeting between the Cougars and Jayhawks was the Aloha Bowl in 1992. Kansas won on a late field goal and subsequent interception from Tom Young.

Just how dynamic is Kansas’ offense?

Scoring-wise, Kansas is 49th in the FBS in points per game. That might not have BYU shaking in their boots, but the Jayhawks can move the ball in many ways. Quarterback Isaiah Marshall only threw three incompletions all game against West Virginia last week. Receivers Nik McMillan and Cam Pickett do most of the damage, accounting for nearly half of the receptions on the team by themselves. Watch out for Nahzae Cox, who is averaging 26.5 yards per catch as a deep threat.

At quarterback, Marshall certainly can hurt defenses with his legs. The signal caller totaled a whopping 164 rushing yards on 19 attempts against the Mountaineers, for an 8.6 yard average. He ranks second in the Big 12 in rushing yards by a quarterback. It’s not just a one-man show on the ground either. Five different Jayhawks carried the football in their 37-14 win over West Virginia. Three different ballcarriers collected at least 14 carries. All this amounts to Kansas boasting the 16th-ranked rushing offense in the FBS.

Where is BYU’s biggest advantage on offense?

Like Kansas, BYU wants to run the ball. LJ Martin is getting healthier each week. Even after not playing during the second half against Baylor, Martin should be good to go for a bigger workload. When facing conference opponents, Kansas ranks 89th in rushing defense, allowing nearly 170 rushing yards per game against Big 12 foes. Kansas’ defense has been generally solid, but this seems like a weak point. The combination of Bear Bachmeier and Martin should get the run game going enough to control the game. BYU also has allowed the third-least sacks among all Power Four teams. The offensive line should be able to hold up against a middling Kansas pass rush.

Kansas is better against the pass, ranking 16th in completion percentage allowed and 47th in passing yards allowed (out of 138).

Are BYU’s road struggles a concern?

BYU’s two losses this season have both come on the road. First, they inexplicably lost to unranked UCF in Orlando. A few weeks ago, Utah defeated the Cougars at Rice-Eccles Stadium. However, those aren’t the only examples of the Cougars struggling on the road this season. Their last road win came in Fort Worth against TCU. TCU came into the game 2-2 and outmatched. Yet it was 7-7 at halftime and the Cougars won by just seven, 17-10.

The Cougars mustered just 216 total yards of offense including a miniscule 62 passing yards. Granted, the weather was very wet and suboptimal for offense. Still, BYU played just as sloppy as the weather, with seven penalties as well. The road struggles are a real thing. That is something BYU needs to overcome. This will not be the most hostile crowd BYU has faced this year, but the Cougars have shown they can come out flat when the game isn’t in Provo.

Do style points matter for BYU?

To put it bluntly, yes. In fact, it might be required. If BYU scrapes by the Jayhawks, the unpredictable committee may punish BYU for playing too close to a 5-6 Kansas team. The spread currently sits at 5.5 points in favor of the Cougars. Winning this game by six points to cover the spread may not be enough. This is because there are two teams just behind BYU in the College Football Playoff rankings hot on their tail. Wake Forest sits at No. 11 with just one loss and a possible trip to the ACC Championship Game in their future. Texas Tech is at 12, likely headed to Arlington. If both of those teams blow out their remaining opponents while BYU inches by Kansas or Cincinnati, the committee may allow one of those teams just behind them to leapfrog the Cougars. The Cougars need to win by double digits.

Prediction: BYU 27, Kansas 23

title: F1's new V8 engine agreed – five things you need to know
summary: F1 will adopt V8 engines in 2030 now key stakeholders have unanimously agreed on key details that will underpin the new rules
reason: F1 locks in a return to V8 engines for 2030, a big rules story.
content_html:
F1's new V8 engine agreed – five things you need to know


Formula 1 will adopt V8 engines in 2030 now key stakeholders have unanimously agreed on the key details that will underpin the new regulations. 

A framework has been unanimously agreed by the FIA, Formula 1, the teams and the engine manufacturers to bring in a 2.1-litre, turbocharged V8 with a reduced electric element.

This switch will be made one year earlier than planned, bringing an early end to the V6 turbo-hybrid rules that only started a controversial new era this season with a switch to a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electric power.  

The FIA World Motor Sport Council will rubber-stamp the plan at a Shanghai meeting next month. 

How key final progress was reached

A meeting of the F1 Commission on Monday, November 16 led to agreement in principle over the framework. 

But it required some final progress to be made for the engine manufacturers themselves to accept ending the current rules cycle in 2029 and be satisfied with the switch. 

The manufacturers are Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull/Ford, Audi Honda and future engine supplier General Motors - which was aiming to belatedly join the current rules cycle before the end of the decade (more on that shortly). 

After the Commission, a meeting with the manufacturers – which are represented in the Commission but have their own key discussion group with the other stakeholders – went through key feedback to resolve what was necessary to push the proposal to the next stage. 

This is what facilitated Friday's announcement of unanimous agreement of the technical framework. 

GM will delay engine to fit

A key consequence of the change of timeline is what it means for GM’s plans. 

Its Cadillac team, which GM is a minority owner of alongside TWG Motorsports, joined the grid this year as a Ferrari customer on the condition it becomes a full works entry. 

GM had been planning to debut that engine built to the current rules in 2029, which it was willing to accept even though it would be only two seasons before all-new rules came in as originally planned. 

To accommodate the next rules era starting earlier, though, GM will delay its manufacturer debut so it does not have to design and build a V6 for one season only.

It is expected to remain a Ferrari customer for an extra year and the rules being agreed is well timed as the purpose-built GM engine facility opens in mid-December this year, which means the full might of its development push can be devoted to the new 2030 rules instead of a split project. 

"For a period of time, we were working on both,” TWG boss Dan Towriss said in Las Vegas. “So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8. There are a number of designs that are in motion now.”

The key details

Officially, the proposed 2030 engine will be a 2.1-litre turbo V8 that carries over “some geometrical specifics”, will feature limited hybridisation” as well as sustainable fuels, and be married to a lighter chassis. 

This is all part of the plan to make the engines simpler, cheaper and louder – although the extent of that last point is still unclear given it will not be a normally aspirated engine. 

“I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps – it's just that high-pitch squeal that I'm missing from this era,” said Mercedes driver George Russell.

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri cautioned “I don't know if they'll be exactly like the V8 engines that I grew up watching, necessarily”, but added “I think it's firstly great that we've been listened to”. 

The turbocharger stays partly to satisfy manufacturer demand but also to assist with fuel efficiency, avoid larger tanks and more fuel usage at the start of races. 

This also helps with the stated aim of making the car and engine around 80kg lighter with almost half of that coming on the engine side. 

More details of this will surely come from the “detailed regulatory framework” that will go to the WMSC in Shanghai next month.

However, it does appear to represent a satisfactory compromise between what some manufacturers want in terms of hybridisation and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem’s initial desire for an even bigger, loud engine without a turbo. 

“The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide,” said Ben Sulayem. 

“Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.”

What’s still to be confirmed

The FIA did not specify the hybrid element, which has been known for some time to be heading towards a 100kW base electric power contribution with an extra 100kW available as effectively a push-to-pass overtaking aid. 

It will give the engine more than 1,000bhp at full power but crucially, compared to the current engines, not be dependent on the electric element and therefore not at the mercy of the energy limitations that have dogged the 2026 rules since their debut. 

Why the hybrid element has not been exactly specified is unclear – “maybe it have some KERS or stuff like that”, as Alpine boss Flavio Briatore put it – but it stands to reason that this is being delayed until more detail can be shared about how it will work. 

With the 2026 rules, the engine regulations were designed first, then the chassis and sporting regulations were contorted around them - leading to a fundamentally compromised product, all because the engine rules had to be set early to get all the targeted manufacturers committed. 

This time the core V8 engine plan should be much simpler to align with the car design and operation, but there are still elements to decide - like exactly how a push-to-pass system should be managed and whether the active aero with movable front and rear wings is worth retaining when that was primarily adopted to assist with making the current cars more efficient on the straights.

Drivers are excited - with minor caveats

Every single driver on the F1 grid has, publicly or privately, expressed their displeasure with the 2026 engines and their consequences. 

So, unsurprisingly, all who have been asked about the return of V8s have welcomed the plan - from the general concept to the fact that there was a good degree of consultation with the drivers themselves. 

Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar said he was very excited for a “full attack racing car” and went as far as adding “I don't see why that would not be the most fun cars of all time in 2030”. 

His team-mate, four-time world champion and vocal 2026 rules critic Max Verstappen, indicated he would have liked it to go further though. 

"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever,” he said. “That sounds even better, but I know that that's not something realistic.

“So this is good, this is for sure in the right direction."

Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton’s own caveat related to the detail of the as-yet undefined regulations that will define how the engines actually work – although what he hopes for most should naturally be achieved simply by stripping back the electric side so much. 

“It's all good and well going to V8, it depends on how they design it, regulation wise,” he said.

“And going back to the good sound because that's I think been lacking since we've been in the V6 era. Bring back the smaller exhaust and get that sound back.

“And as long as we don't have the engine dying halfway down the straight, then I think that will be better.”

title: Signal Blocks AI Agents From Reading Private Chats via Screenshots on Android and iOS
summary: Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete." The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal
reason: Signal is defending end-to-end encryption against on-device AI agents in iOS 27, a new frontier for private messaging.
content_html:
Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete."

The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen.

It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature.

Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

"The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy."

The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk.

Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android).

"However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said.

"Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system."

Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data.

Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users -

  • Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience
  • Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing

The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup.

On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications.

In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post.

"We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said.

"In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents."

Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings.

Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

Google News,

title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
summary: A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown. The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts. reason: A one-page attack on an AI assistant's memory and connected credentials shows how agent security is breaking down.
content_html:
A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.

The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.

The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.

There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.

Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage."

In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up.

From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown.

That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent.

The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines.

Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through.

The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in.

The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
summary: A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG. The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0,
reason: A critical bug in the library most apps use to handle OpenPGP keys, triggered just by importing a hostile key.
content_html:
A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG.

The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program.

Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages.

The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.

Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says.

The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG.

When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details.

The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier.

What to Update

The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

What to install depends on where the library sits:

  • Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory.
  • Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible.
  • Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch.
  • Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases.
  • GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed.

The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.

title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access
summary: Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week. The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup,
reason: Amazon reports attackers using autonomous AI agents to find and exploit a zero-day, a real milestone for offensive AI.
content_html:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.

The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.

The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.

MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.

The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.

The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.

Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.

Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.

The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.

Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.

A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.

That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.

In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.

The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.

Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.

The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw.

What to Do Now

With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach:

  • Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs.
  • Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default.
  • Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to.
  • Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched.
  • If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used.

The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described.

The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.

title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
reason: A ransomware recovery firm that claimed crypto magic was just paying the attackers, a great Krebs cautionary tale.
content_html:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

title: There’s Something Weird Going On at Apple
summary: If you’re paying attention, there’s something weird going on at Apple lately. On the most recent MacBook Pro, the PROLED model, they put the glowing Apple logo back in the lid. reason: MacSparky reads the tea leaves on Apple's recent turn toward delight and whimsy under John Ternus.
content_html:
If you’re paying attention, there’s something weird going on at Apple lately.

On the most recent MacBook Pro, the PROLED model, they put the glowing Apple logo back in the lid. The CEO, John Ternus, even commented on that in a recent interview with Steven Levy, where he bragged about it.

When Siri AI released, a lot of us were complaining that it didn’t have enough third-party support and third-party app developers had their hands tied. Applying our traditional Apple thinking caps, we all figured that at the soonest we’d get a little bit more access next June, but this would take years. Yet that expanded third-party access is already showing up in the point release betas.

After the iPhone Duo released, a lot of people complained they wished it had Face ID. Well, the device doesn’t have hardware for that, but it does have a front-facing camera. And in the latest point release for the iPhone Duo, Apple’s turned on a form of face identification. It doesn’t work for everything because it’s not as secure as Face ID, but it is something a user can select to get to their phone more quickly.

It just seems Apple lately is a lot more nimble with their updates and responsiveness.

Maybe this is just a weird set of coincidences. But I’d like to attribute it to John Ternus. He is, after all, a product guy. And I can’t help but think that he uses and cares about these things more than Tim Cook did.

This isn’t meant to be a dig on Tim Cook. He did his job. And the company became a lot bigger and more profitable under his watch, but I’m not in it for the stock price. I’m in it for the user experience, and lately I’m noticing things.

I almost didn’t create this newsletter out of fear that I would jinx it all, but we may be entering a new phase with Apple products where things are a bit more delightful. I sure hope that’s the case.

The post There’s Something Weird Going On at Apple appeared first on MacSparky.

title: Emergent properties
summary: No system stays the way it began, and all systems evolve characteristics that surprise us. The rise of the automobile system led to roads and gas stations, of course, but also parking lots, drive-through fast food restaurants and drunk driving. The TV industrial complex was based on the effectiveness of advertising, and the ads that […]
reason: Seth Godin on how systems grow surprising side effects, a useful lens for anyone shaping a platform.
content_html:
Emergent properties

No system stays the way it began, and all systems evolve characteristics that surprise us.

The rise of the automobile system led to roads and gas stations, of course, but also parking lots, drive-through fast food restaurants and drunk driving.

The TV industrial complex was based on the effectiveness of advertising, and the ads that were among the most profitable were for beverages and snack foods, which made those industries ever more efficient and led to convenience foods and also widespread obesity.

And factory farming feeds billions of people. Competitive pressures led to a rise in fertilizer use and a destruction of topsoil, which also dramatically shifts the climate.

Any complex system will soon surprise us with its unanticipated effects.

title: Penalised Antonelli beats Verstappen with both Ferraris out in Q2
summary: Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying at F1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, but Max Verstappen will start from pole position, and both Ferraris missed the pole battle
reason: Las Vegas GP qualifying chaos puts Verstappen on pole despite Antonelli's top lap, ahead of tonight's race.
content_html:
Penalised Antonelli beats Verstappen with both Ferraris out in Q2

Kimi Antonelli topped qualifying at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, but Max Verstappen will start from pole position because of the Mercedes driver’s grid penalty, and both Ferraris failed to make the pole fight.

Antonelli has a five-place grid penalty for taking the updated Mercedes ADUO turbocharger this weekend, but he minimised the damage of that beautifully in Q3.

Antonelli gambled by dropping back from a squabbling pack of cars on the final runs as he ended up crossing the line with only a couple of seconds to spare.

But that turned out perfectly as he was in the ideal track position to pick up a huge slipstream from multiple cars at the end of the lap to set a 1m33.893s.

That was two and a half tenths quicker than Max Verstappen, who couldn’t improve on his second Q3 run.

But he’ll start from pole position because of Antonelli’s penalty and will share the front row of the grid with the man he clashed with in practice, George Russell.

Russell asked Mercedes for a tow from Antonelli, which didn’t transpire.

Lando Norris was fourth for McLaren ahead of Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls, who was a career-best sixth.

Oscar Piastri was seventh but he has to serve a 10-place grid penalty.

Liam Lawson was eighth ahead of Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, who had been second in Q2. Team-mate Franco Colapinto rounded out the top 10, after brushing the wall.

Both Ferraris out in Q2

The biggest shock of qualifying proved to be a double Ferrari Q2 elimination, the first time the team has failed to get a car into Q3 since Imola last year.

Lewis Hamilton was struggling throughout FP3 and qualifying, and looked vulnerable to an early exit from the start.

But team-mate Charles Leclerc ended up joining him in the danger zone after he made an error into Turn 7, ruined his lap and then fell short of making the chequered flag for another attempt.

As others improved, that meant Leclerc and Hamilton were shuffled down to 11th and 12th.

Behind them were the Audis and Williams, with Nico Hulkenberg leading Carlos Sainz, Gabriel Bortoleto and Alex Albon.

Rafael Camara was knocked out in 17th in his second-ever F1 qualifying session, seven hundredths away from a second successive Q2 session.

Sergio Perez was 18th for Cadillac - his best qualifying since Monaco - even though he was left without a tow from his team-mate Valtteri Bottas on his lap, as in Bottas’s words, “We lost each other.”

Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll were 19th and 20th for Aston Martin, ahead of Bottas and Bearman, who sacrificed his qualifying session to tow Camara, because of his huge grid penalty.

title: ★ A Week With the New Privacy Controls in MacOS 27.3 Beta 2
summary: On Monday, when the second betas of the v27.3 OSes came out, I posted about Apple adding the new privacy controls they had promised a month prior , in the wake of Meta’s Muse app surprising some users with what information it had access to (e.g., incoming iMessages) after being granted Full Disk Access — which authorization some users just clicked right through. reason: Gruber's hands-on look at Apple's new Full Disk Access privacy controls, squarely in Apple security territory.
content_html:
On Monday, when the second betas of the v27.3 OSes came out, I posted about Apple adding the new privacy controls they had promised a month prior, in the wake of Meta’s Muse app surprising some users with what information it had access to (e.g., incoming iMessages) after being granted Full Disk Access — which authorization some users just clicked right through. I also posted a link to Apple’s corresponding new support documents. My initial take on Monday:

I’m installing it now, but from what I’ve seen so far, these changes not only alleviate my concerns that Apple might over-tighten the screws, I actually think they add clarity and give users more, not less, control over their Macs.

After a week, I’m willing to call it: this overhaul of these settings and permissions is a win. I really like the way that, for apps asking for Full Disk Access, users can now grant access to a list of folders instead. That’s what I mean about these new settings giving users more control.

Are these new dialog boxes “scarier”? Yes, and the point is, they should be. You should be slightly jolted into attention when an app prompts for any of these permissions. The question is whether they are unnecessarily scary. I would say no, not at all. The descriptions are fair and accurate. Is it unnecessarily scary to show you thumbnails of your personal photos before permitting Full Disk Access that would grant an application unfettered access to your personal photos? No! It’s a bit of a jolt to see them, but that’s just reducing the abstraction. The words “full disk access” feel different than actually seeing a snapshot of what full disk access entails.

Might this discourage some Mac users from granting Full Disk Access to AI agent apps? Yes. And it should! Users who actually understand the stakes will not be dissuaded by these new permissions — when granting them is what they know they want to do. Additionally, I think these new dialog boxes represent very good UI design. They look like a new modern take on MacOS “system chrome” design — not skinny iPhone-sized alerts.

My only gripe about the new stuff is the prominent menu bar indicator that now appears when one app is controlling another. You can’t turn it off (except via an undocumented hidden defaults setting), and it’s distracting on most Macs, and extra distracting on the new MacBook Pros with PROLED displays because on those Macs, it appears in the Dynamic Island! Chance Miller, on Threads (with screenshots):

Most of the changes in macOS 27.3 are reasonable, but this Live Activity thing for system access has got to go. It’s way too aggressive.

It takes over the Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro!

As I write this article on a new MacBook Pro review unit, I have 8 of these indicators in my Dynamic Island: Scroll Reverser, Keyboard Maestro Engine, HazeOver, SteerMouse Manager, Moom, Chest (a promising new utility for managing menu bar icons), System Events, and a new text snippet expansion utility I’m beta testing.

Every one of these apps is running all of the time for me. This indicator being on, all the time, for every one of them isn’t helping me notice unusual activity. If anything, if Apple doesn’t rethink this idea, it’s going to make me miss the indication if an app is taking advantage of access permissions in an unwanted or unexpected way.

Zac Hall, Miller’s colleague at 9to5Mac, published an article on Tuesday showing the command-line defaults incantation to disable this. That’s better than not being able to disable it at all, but I expect Apple to revisit this based on feedback. It seems like a well-intentioned feature that was designed by people who didn’t realize how many always-on utilities “control other apps”.
