content_html:
Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.

Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.

OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.

The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.

The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.

The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.

The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.

One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.

On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.

"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.

The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.

The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.

One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.

A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.

A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint.

Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt.

In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings.

OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.

The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties.

The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week.

Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers.

Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted.

What the Providers Have Disclosed

An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections.

Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated.

A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window.

At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July.

The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts.

Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers.

Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three.

The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week.

What Users Should Do

The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price.

Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check.

Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys.

A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.

title: Nothing Brite about it
summary: Siri’s great failing over the past decade and a half has been its contextual ignorance . It treated every request you made as if it were the first chalk markings on a great blank slate, a slate that was immediately washed clean after it answered you. That’s no longer the case with Siri AI. It now keeps track of your conversations, and it can dig through your apps to find information. This is, without question, a tremendous improvement, but I did run into a problem with it about a week ago.
reason: Dr. Drang's thoughtful take on how Siri AI finally keeps conversational context, and where it still falls short.
content_html:
Siri’s great failing over the past decade and a half has been its contextual ignorance. It treated every request you made as if it were the first chalk markings on a great blank slate, a slate that was immediately washed clean after it answered you. That’s no longer the case with Siri AI. It now keeps track of your conversations, and it can dig through your apps to find information. This is, without question, a tremendous improvement, but I did run into a problem with it about a week ago.

I was out on a walk, listening to one of Apple Music’s built-in playlists, and “I’m Just a Singer (In a Rock and Roll Band)” by the Moody Blues came on. I wasn’t paying close attention, but after a while I realized that I didn’t know who the lead singer was. I knew only that it wasn’t Justin Hayward, who did most of their lead vocals. So I asked Siri, “Who’s singing lead vocals on this song?”

This was a test. I would never have asked the pre-2025 Siri this kind of question. I have asked similar questions over the past year or two, but only because I figured Siri would pass the question along to ChatGPT. And in those cases, I made the question more explicit—something like “Who is the lead singer on the Moody Blues song ‘I’m Just a Singer (In a Rock and Roll Band)’?”—because Siri usually wouldn’t tell ChatGPT what I was listening to.

Siri AI passed the test, telling me it was John Lodge. Great! I decided to do this more often.

A couple of minutes later, “Do It Again” by Steely Dan started playing.1 I had a vague memory of seeing a video of them performing this song on some TV show, with Skunk Baxter playing bongos. Was that just for the TV show, or did he also play bongos on the record? So I asked Siri, “Who’s playing percussion2 on this song?”

Siri answered that Graeme Edge played percussion on “I’m Just a Singer (In a Rock and Roll Band).” A correct answer, but not what I was looking for. I wondered if Siri was running slow and hadn’t updated itself to know what the current song was. So I asked again and got the same answer. Then I asked for the lead vocalist and got an answer of John Lodge again. What the hell?

Then I realized that I had been caught by conversational context. After my first question, in which Siri correctly interpreted “this song” as the song that was currently playing, it treated my later questions as part of an extended conversation about “I’m Just a Singer” and interpreted “this song” accordingly. So I changed my question to “Who is playing percussion on the currently playing song?” This switched Siri’s context, and I got the right answer. (It was V. Feldman, not Skunk Baxter, although Baxter did play guitar on the track.)

I suspect that if more time had passed between the two songs (and my questions), Siri would have changed its interpretation of “this song.” How much time? I have no idea. Despite what George Harrison told us, “this song” has something tricky about it.

  1. No, the music you listen to is shit. ↩

  2. I thought “percussion” was more likely than “bongos” to be in the song credits. ↩

reason: A Big Think essay on Epicurean decision-making, the kind of good-life philosophy Jack saves.
content_html:
You are able to make good decisions about how to live your life.

I hate to open a new newsletter with a twee self-help aphorism covered in fortune cookie crumbs, but it’s probably the most important thing to start with. Because Epicureanism is an ancient Greek philosophy, and like almost all its contemporaries, it places responsibility on you. You are the overseer of your life. You can think things through, make good choices, and get things right. You are not some child, carried about by adult hands, blinking at a world blurring by. In the eyes of Greek philosophers, you are a rational, intelligent, deliberative human being. You control your life.

Epicureanism argues that a good life is one where we develop strategies to either cure or endure pain — both physical and emotional — while seeking out opportunities to enjoy ourselves more. It says that a happy life means savoring simple pleasures where you are, right now, and with the people who matter. But to do that, we need to make better decisions. We need to willfully choose an Epicurean life. We need to work at happiness.

Some of you might be wondering why there’s a cute little crab scuttling along our freshly minted logo. Well, that’s a hermit crab. In my upcoming book, The Art of Enough, I use the hermit crab motif to represent one of the most important ideas in Epicureanism. Because I think it embodies a certain skill we all need to nurture if we are to live a good life.

summary: The single most important factor in learning is whether the student is actively engaged in the process. Eyes bright, hands up, curious and eager for the insight on the other side. Ask any teacher–students like this are a delight. The same is true for the work of professionals–from doctors to cashiers. Wanting to be there, […]
reason: Seth Godin on why engagement has to be earned, useful for leading teams and PMs.
content_html:
The single most important factor in learning is whether the student is actively engaged in the process.

Eyes bright, hands up, curious and eager for the insight on the other side.

Ask any teacher–students like this are a delight.

The same is true for the work of professionals–from doctors to cashiers. Wanting to be there, open to interaction, eager for change–these are so obvious that we usually overlook them.

In fact, the real work of anyone building an institution of learning or an organization that seeks to serve is simple: create the conditions for people to choose to actively participate.

The lazy method is to wait for the self-motivated and take credit for the results when they show up. The hard work is to build the systems and culture that makes it more likely that you’re attracting, motivating and transforming the people who want to go where you can take them.

Everything else is a bonus.

content_html:
You probably said some choice words, but a Bear Bachmeier two-point conversion completion to JoJo Phillips in triple overtime lifted BYU in a 31-29 win over Kansas Saturday in Lawrence.

BYU went into half down 6-3, but two third quarter interceptions from the defense allowed BYU to pull ahead 16-6 going into the fourth quarter. Kansas tied the game, and Matthias Dunn shanked a kick on the last play of regulation.

Kansas has played teams tight this year, but it doesn’t feel good to scrape by a 4-6 team. LJ Martin played most of the game, and while he was bottled up for much of the game, came through in the end and ran for 127 yards. Bear Bachmeier passed for 173 yards and added 59 rushing yards and 2 rushing TDs.

Stats were even across the board, which is not surprising considering the result. Both teams had 2 turnovers and outgained Kansas 381-359.

Next we’ll see how the committee treats BYU after the result. Regardless, BYU’s CFP and Big 12 title game hopes remain alive when BYU hosts Cincinnati next Saturday in the final regular season game.

title: Verstappen wins breathless Las Vegas GP as Ferraris collide
summary: Max Verstappen delivered a masterclass to win a peloton-style Las Vegas GP, while George Russell crashed and the Ferrari drivers collided
reason: Verstappen won a wild Las Vegas GP with 20-plus lead changes while the Ferraris collided.
content_html:
Verstappen wins breathless Las Vegas GP as Ferraris collide

Max Verstappen delivered a masterclass in defensive driving to win a peloton-style Las Vegas Grand Prix for Red Bull, while main challenger George Russell crashed and the Ferrari drivers collided amid their recent struggles.

The first 15 laps were manic with the slipstream proving so powerful that constant changes of position took place, as Russell took the lead three times at the Turn 14 chicane only to be repassed before or into Turn 1 by Verstappen each time.

Isack Hadjar had also ran second and attacked Verstappen, and begged Red Bull to instruct Verstappen not to defend so that they could pass and repass each other to try to break away, but he predicted on the radio he was about to be passed by Russell and so it proved.

The yo-yoing changed on lap 15 because the top five at that point - Verstappen, Russell, Hadjar, Pierre Gasly and Kimi Antonelli - stopped fighting long enough to break clear of Arvid Lindblad, creating a buffer to the rest of the field and allowing these cars to escape before a safety car for Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara's collision at Turn 14, which left Perez in the barrier.

After a seven-lap delay for barrier repairs that included a full set of pitstops, immediately after the restart Hadjar's front wing failed taking him out of contention, and Verstappen and Russell went at it with another three lead changes, as Lando Norris - 11th earlier in the race - and Antonelli, on an opposite tyre strategy on the softs to finish the race, took turns in the lead before being dispatched again.

On Russell in particular, Verstappen pulled off two incredible instances of going around the outside at Turn 2 and one dive at Turn 5 to retake the lead, completing most of his overtaking in the corners versus many others doing most of their work on the straights.

Antonelli established himself as Verstappen's main threat in the closing stages, especially after Russell locked up and went into the barrier at Turn 5 with three laps to go, remarkably getting going again to finish in the points.

And then Antonelli lost positions to both McLarens going into Turn 1 on the final lap, suffering for lifting to stay behind Verstappen, which had deployment consequences.

That buffer gave Verstappen - who laughed and mocked Russell (with whom he'd clashed in FP3 on Friday) on the radio with a "well done" after his crash - a crucial one-second lead that he was able to eke out into victory across the line.

During the safety car McLaren CEO Zak Brown sounded defeated when speaking to Sky Sports F1 after Norris had dropped as low as 11th, but the fastest lap in the first stint showed the McLaren driver's pace and an excellent recovery from him and Piastri - up 14 places - was rewarded with a double-podium. "Who would have thought?" said Norris at that result.

Antonelli just held on for fourth after his power issues, repassing Gasly into the chicane on the final lap to secure the position.

Fifth was nevertheless Gasly's best result of the season, while Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto was elevated to sixth in the final classification as the team clawed back 18 points against Racing Bulls.

Lewis Hamilton ended as the top Ferrari driver in seventh in a bitter display for the Scuderia as its drivers both lost a sack full of positions and crashed into each other during this race as their teamwork issues continue.

The Ferraris had bickered in the first stint as Hamilton had an expletive-led rant about how Leclerc needed to work with him to overtake, while Leclerc accused Hamilton of "squeezing" him and said that would "end badly" if it carried on.

Hamilton was given a 10-second penalty for going off track in a battle with Norris, which he served under the safety car, and fought back to lead Leclerc afterwards, before Leclerc spun Hamilton out at Turn 7 - which the stewards gave Leclerc a 10-second penalty for.

Leclerc had been sixth on the road before the penalty.

His dropping down to 10th helped Carlos Sainz give Williams its joint-best result of the year at one of the few tracks it hadn't written off at the end of the season, while his team-mate Alex Albon was not able to start the race.

Russell was just behind him in ninth and Leclerc rounded out the top 10 after his penalty, ahead of the Audis of Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto.

Lindblad had been fifth in the queue under the safety car but spun while trying to generate heat in his tyres and ultimately retired from the race, meaning Racing Bulls failed to score any points - Liam Lawson starting the race a lap down and recovering to 15th, one place behind Hadjar.

content_html:
My first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass, were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing, the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing (and classic Mac OS).

After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales).

Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace, which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files. Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse!

Alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner.

This is not a hard problem to solve. Plenty of Mac apps can provide something close to what I want…but not exactly what I want, in the specific way that I want it. For many years, I got by with some folders in the corner of my desktop. But the problem nagged at me.

A few years ago, I went so far as to implement my desired feature in SwitchGlass, adding the ability to create a small, extra palette full of folders in addition to the app switcher. But it felt incongruous with the rest of the app, so I never shipped it. And I didn’t want to maintain my own private fork of SwitchGlass, so I abandoned that branch of the code.

How It Started

Today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of new, niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. Even for experienced software developers, vibe coding has made it possible to create apps that were previously “not worth building” due to an unfavorable ratio of effort to payoff.

It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right?

That was three and a half months ago.

How It’s Going

So what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed.

I began the project by feeding a coding agent the source code to my app, SwitchGlass, as a starting point. I wrote SwitchGlass six years ago using a substantially more primitive version of SwiftUI. (For the developers out there, it predates @Observable and @State, and it supports Macs all the way back to macOS 12 Monterey from 2021.) I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display.

It worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess…

Now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock.

Only Apple…

If you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews, you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.)

To pick just one example, I’ve always wanted clicking on a folder in the Dock to open that folder in the Finder. The Dock did work this way for several years, but in 2009’s Mac OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard (…I think?), Apple switched to requiring a Command-Option-click to open a folder in the Finder. Since then, I’ve been Command-Option-clicking folders in the Dock many, many times per day. It’s a small thing, but it adds up: seventeen years of Command-Option clicking!

But what could I do? I was forced to continue to use the Dock because there are so many things that “only the Dock can do” in macOS. I was reminded of this harsh reality when I created SwitchGlass. Why doesn’t SwitchGlass show notification badges? Why does the Calendar icon show today’s date in the Dock but not in SwitchGlass? Why don’t app icons in SwitchGlass bounce when the app needs attention? Why can’t I quit an app from SwitchGlass?

Though I did find a workaround for that last one, the answer to most of these questions is that third-party apps simply can’t do all the things the Dock can do. The Dock is part of the operating system, and it enjoys special privileges and deep integration that no third-party app can match.

This remains true today, especially for sandboxed apps sold through the Mac App Store like SwitchGlass (and all my other Mac apps). But what about apps that aren’t in the Mac App Store? What about unsandboxed apps? How close can they come to doing all the things the Dock does, especially if they use private APIs that are forbidden in the Mac App Store?

I aimed to find out. I hatched a plan, which I announced on episode 706 of Accidental Tech Podcast on August 26, 2026. I would create two apps: one called Jetty that would be sold through the Mac App Store, and a more powerful, unsandboxed app called Jetty Pro that would be distributed directly to customers, outside the Mac App Store.

But as I worked on the two apps, it became clear that “plain Jetty” was not that great. It had all the same limitations as SwitchGlass when it came to duplicating the features of the Dock. After less than two weeks of work, I abandoned plain Jetty and concentrated entirely on Jetty Pro.

After three and a half months of work, there are still things that only the Dock can do, but the list is not very long. I don’t expect most users to fully replace the Dock with Jetty Pro, but I’m happily doing so. If only my 2001 self could see me now!

The Jetty Pro icon, created by The Iconfactory

Jetty Pro

Now, finally, I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to. Here are some of the highlights:

  • Jetty Pro palettes are extensively customizable. Nearly every palette layout metric can be adjusted. Jetty Pro can simulate the Dock backgrounds from macOS 15, 26, and 27, and it provides several of its own background appearances as well. The image at the top of this post shows just some of the possibilities.

  • Jetty Pro lets you customize the icon of any item in a palette—even the Finder. And if you’ve ever wanted to break an app out of Squircle Jail, now you can do it.

  • Unlike the macOS Dock, Jetty Pro will show folder label colors (without also setting a folder symbol). You can even apply color labels to folders independent of their labels in the Finder.

  • Don’t want to see “Running in Background” apps in macOS 27? Jetty Pro can hide them.

  • Want to hide notification badges for specific apps, but only in specific palettes? Jetty Pro can do that. And unlike the Dock, Jetty Pro can even hide notification badges on the System Settings app.

  • Jetty Pro can exclude or include running apps of your choice on a per-palette basis.

  • Jetty Pro lets you choose what happens when you click (or modifier-click) an app or folder in a palette.

  • A Jetty Pro palette can be configured to appear on a single display, selected displays, or on every display, while also choosing which attributes, like size and position, are allowed to vary per display.

  • Use Jetty Pro to augment the macOS Dock with additional palettes, or use it to replace the Dock entirely. It’s up to you.

Jetty Pro is available for a special introductory price of $9.99 per year (plus applicable taxes) until the end of 2026, with a 14-day free trial.

Download Jetty Pro 14-day Free Trial

To learn more, including why a subscription is the only way to pay for Jetty Pro, please read the extensive documentation.

As you might have already guessed, Jetty Pro uses every private API it can get its hands on, and it requires a ton of special permissions, all of which are explained in the documentation. For sensible security reasons, macOS makes it (increasingly) cumbersome for users to grant these permissions. But Jetty Pro needs them to do what it does. Check Settings > General in Jetty Pro and make sure it says “All permissions have been granted” at the bottom. If not, click the “Details…” button for further instructions.

After a brief dalliance with more “mainstream” apps like Hyperspace, I’m back to making niche apps for Mac weirdos like me. To thine own self be true, I guess. I hope there are others out there who have longed to make the Dock work just slightly differently and are now able to do so thanks to Jetty Pro.

I’m sure many people reading this will think it’s ridiculous that I spent months battling the limitations of macOS to create what appears (to the undiscerning eye) to be a nearly identical clone of the Dock. What a waste of time! And what took so long anyway? This is a weekend project, at most!

First, I can assure you that the “simple” appearance of Jetty Pro belies the huge level of complexity and trickery required to do so many different things that macOS does not support and actively works against. If Jetty Pro really does seem simple in use, then I have done my job well. (And if you can see the seams, then that’s where I’ve failed to completely overcome a hostile system that doesn’t want to allow Jetty Pro to do what it needs to do.)

Second, I put a tremendous amount of time and effort into Jetty Pro. The documentation alone (which, like every word in every post on this website, was written by me and me alone) took weeks to create. During the lead up to Jetty Pro 1.0, I’ve released over 160 builds to my 250 beta testers—more than one build per day. The Jetty Pro app icon was created by the fine humans at The Iconfactory. From the start, I’ve treated Jetty Pro like a “real” app, not a throwaway vibe-coded project.

Having spent so many years with the Dock as a tiny pebble in my shoe, the difference between it and Jetty Pro means everything to me. Like Front and Center and SwitchGlass before it, I’m now running Jetty Pro all day, every day on my Mac. Replacing the Dock with Jetty Pro has made me happier than any other app I’ve created. I hope it will make some other Mac weirdos happy too.

reason: On your always-include list.
content_html:
Some in the traditional media have gone wild about it, with near-apocalyptic predictions of the impacts of the current very strong El Nino.

Many on social media have predicted disaster for our region.

The data suggests they are wrong... and this blog provides some of the evidence.


You have heard the litany of "Super" El Nino problems for the Northwest and California:  there will be drought or flooding. Lack of snowpack or excessive snow.  That the reservoirs will be emptied or overtopped.

These El Nino disaster predictions are not reliable. 

Some depend on extended-range weather/climate models, which are notoriously unskillful.  

Some forecasts are based on El Niños that are moderate or strong.  This does not work because very strong or "super "El Niño events are different animals in terms of their impacts on the Pacific Northwest.  

In this blog,  I will use the most reliable approach: considering only years with a very strong El Niño: 1982-1984, 1997-1998, and 2015-2016.  The true analogs to this year.

Let's start by examining precipitation in Seattle for the very strong El Nino years.   

In the figures below, green indicates the cumulative precipitation from Sept 1 to June 1 for the very strong El Nino year in question, and purple shows the climatological average values considering all years.

For the 1982-1983 event, cool-season precipitation ended up near normal, with a drier-than-normal November (sounds familiar?), but wetter than normal late winter.



The 1997-1998 very strong El Nino cool season ended up slightly drier than normal after a normal winter.


2015-2016 was considerably wetter than normal.


So, the analogous past very strong El Nino years showed NO tendency for a dry winter in Seattle (or generally anywhere in our region). 

 NO REASON TO PANIC.

What about temperature in Seattle during the very strong El Nino years?  

The plots below show the observed temperatures (blue) for the winter season, with red indicating extreme highs and light blue showing record lows. The climatological (average)  temperature range is indicated by the brown band.

For the 1982-1983 very strong El Nino, temperatures were on the warm side in early autumn, below normal in November and December, and moderately above normal during the rest of the year. Yawn.  


1997-1998 was overall normal regarding temperature, with a few warm and cold periods.


2015-16 was near normal below February 1 but warmer than normal during spring


Overall, Seattle temperatures for strong El Nino winters were skewed modestly warm, but with plenty of below-normal interludes.

What about Northwest snowpack (on April 1 for each year)?  Folks are REALLY worried about the snowpack this year.

 The answer is found below, with the strong El Nino years indicated by the red arrows.  

Shocking.  Very strong El Nino years have ended up with near-average regional snowpack at the official observing locations.

Want a more general view of the impacts of very strong El Nino years over the western U.S. and the region?  

Below are NOAA graphics for the entire nation!

For September to June precipitation, the entire West Coast is wetter than normal, which is good for filling reservoirs and supporting healthy streamflow.   


As expected for an El Nino year, Northern California does particularly well, which is excellent for filling the many large California reservoirs in that region.   Southern Oregon
 is very wet as well.  

Very encouraging for California agriculture and weather supplies.

What about temperature during strong El Nino years?  Shown below.

Away from the coast, California is cooler than normal. Nevada and Colorado are cold.  

That means massive snowfall in the Sierra Nevada, for the Colorado River drainage, and around the LA basin.   Good news for water resources. 

Washington State is warmer than normal, but the western slopes of the Cascades are only modestly warm.  With the expected normal to above-normal precipitation, this implies only a modest reduction in snowpack, consistent with the snowpack statistics I provided above. 



In summary, a very strong El Nino year provides no reason to be alarmed along the West Coast regarding water resources, at least if past "super" El Nino years are a guide.    

The media and many amateur weather sites (especially a certain name-calling YouTube site) are making serious errors in their predictions based on weaker El Niño events.

title: M6 iMac Review: Apple’s latest power play
summary: I don’t remember the last desktop Macintosh I used as my full-time computer — probably whatever Mac was at my desk at the weekly newspaper I worked at in 1994.…
reason: Jason Snell's full review of the new M6 iMac, the big Apple hardware read of the day.
content_html:
I don’t remember the last desktop Macintosh I used as my full-time computer — probably whatever Mac was at my desk at the weekly newspaper I worked at in 1994. (A Macintosh Classic II, maybe? Sure. Let’s go with that.) When it came time to buy a computer of my own, I selected a PowerBook with my college graduation money, figuring my career path as a roving reporter would benefit from having a machine that could go with me. And it’s been a series of laptops ever since then, from iBooks to MacBook Pros to MacBook Airs.

The point is, after I opened the very large box Jason had dropped off at my front door and sat down to put Apple’s new M6 iMac through its paces, it was the first time in a long time that I’ve used a desktop Mac for more than just a brief period. A big display, a beefy processor and all the ports I could ever want before having to plug into hubs and dongles — a fellow could get used to living like this.

That said, as much as I’ve enjoyed my time with the iMac, I’m not about to abandon the freedom of mobile computing in exchange for the power boost that comes from a more sedentary lifestyle. But for anyone more committed to desktops over laptops, there’s a lot to like about Apple’s latest iMac, especially if you’ve gone a few years in between upgrades.

Apple’s previous iMac, an M4-powered all-in-one, came out two years ago, and you’re not going to spot many differences between that version and the latest model. Even owners of 2023’s M3 iMac aren’t likely to be moved by this latest edition.

But if you’re making do with an iMac powered by an M1 chip — or, heaven forfend, a model that predates the move to Apple Silicon — the M6 iMac promises to be a significant upgrade over what you have. And the M6 processor running the show is a big reason why.

All about the M6

If I had the space on my desk to accommodate both an M6 iMac and the M4 iMac it replaces in Apple’s lineup, I wouldn’t be able to spot any surface changes. Like its predecessor, the M6 iMac offers a 24-inch Retina display with 4.5K resolution. The display still promises 500 nits of brightness, and the 21.5-by-18.1-inch frame and 5.8-inch-deep stand go unchanged. Apple’s even offering the same seven color options as before, with my review unit coming in a fetching purple.

The big changes come under the hood in the form of that M6 processor, which offers a new mix of cores and two Neural Engines, providing tangible boosts over the M4.

Like I said, though, M4 iMac owners are unlikely to be eyeballing the new machine with envy, especially since Apple upped the base price on the iMac by $200 to $1,499 back in June, and that price is maintained by the new M6 model.

M6 iMac performance notes

To that end, Apple’s promising a 5x improvement in AI workflows from the M4 iMac, courtesy of those Neural Engines. Obviously, anyone moving from an Intel-based Mac can expect a dramatic increase in performance, and early-generation Apple silicon Mac users will also see solid benefits. I don’t have any comparable all-in-ones lying around my house, but I do own an M3 MacBook Air equipped with 8GB of RAM, and the M6 iMac with 16GB of RAM that I’m testing smokes that laptop, as you might expect.

Specifically, when I ran Geekbench 7 on both machines, the M6 iMac posted single and multicore scores of 3,967 and 21,078, respectively. Those results beat the comparable numbers posted by my MacBook Air by 39% and 87%. Likewise, the M6 iMac’s GPU score was just about 4x better than what the laptop could put out.

To put that in real-world terms, the M6 chip powering the latest iMac is perfectly capable of handling whatever you want to throw at it. You can also expect smooth, detailed graphics when you’re playing games.

That processing muscle also comes into play when you’re handling tasks like editing photos, which was a breeze for me on the M6 iMac. Also helping matters is that display, which really calls out the subtle nuances of an image better than smaller screens, even my MacBook Air, as good as its 13-inch Liquid Retina display may be on its own.

After all, the entire idea behind the iMac is that it can satisfy people who want a desktop but don’t necessarily need the power (and price tag) that comes with a Mac Studio. That could include creative pros whose hardware budget tops out at around $2,000 as well as families who need a dependable machine that multiple people can turn to.

The other iMac changes

The M6 is easily the most substantive change Apple made to this version of the iMac, but it’s not the only under-the-hood improvement. The M6 iMac also features Apple’s N1 chip, which supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. The M4 iMac’s wireless specs topped out at Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3.

Like Wi-Fi 6E, Wi-Fi 7 supports 6GHz, 5GHz and 2.4GHz bands, but with greater bandwidth and wider channels. It’s also capable of delivering faster wireless speeds, while support for Multi-Link Operation means your iMac can send and receive data across different bands. The end result is better, more efficient throughput.

Of course, for your M6 iMac to reap the full benefits of Wi-Fi 7, you’re going to need to connect to a Wi-Fi 7 router. Maybe you’ve recently upgraded your networking equipment to support the latest standards, maybe you haven’t. But even if it’s the latter, the M6 iMac’s support for the latest wireless connectivity standards means you’ve future-proofed your computer for your next purchase of a router or access point.

Configuring your M6 iMac

As noted above, the M6 iMac starts at $1,499. That gets you a machine with a 10-core CPU and GPU chip along with two rear Thunderbolt ports, 16GB of memory and 256GB of storage.

That’s not the machine I tested. Instead, my review unit came with the 12-core M6 chip and four Thunderbolt ports. That also means a 2.5Gb Ethernet port is included on my iMac; for the two-port models, it’s a $30 add-on. My machine came configured with the standard 16GB of RAM, but storage space was upgraded to 512GB. As configured, that machine would set you back $1,899. If you maxed out the memory and storage while also adding nano-texture glass to reduce glare and reflections on the display, you could pay as much as $3,299 for your all-in-one Mac.

As for that nano-texture option, I really didn’t miss it on my iMac, but I had the luxury of testing the machine in a basement office without much in the way of harsh lighting, either from the overhead lights or the window in the room facing away from the Mac. If you set up your computer in less forgiving settings — a cubicle, say, or a desk next to a window — that $200 nano-texture add-on (only available on the higher-end configurations) might save you a lot of squinting and a little bit of buyer’s remorse.

Making sense of the iMac

The M6 iMac doesn’t reinvent Apple’s all-in-one offering so much as it restates things, adding a more advanced processor, improved wireless connectivity and not much else. That’s not a criticism — just an honest assessment of who should consider making this particular machine their next Mac.

If it’s been more than three or four years since you’ve last upgraded your desktop, the M6 iMac offers enough horsepower to justify getting a new machine. And if this would be your first Mac all-in-one after trying out other computing options — a long line of laptops, say — this is a solid iteration for the iMac lineup.

title: Government Regulation and Demand
summary: Last week I linked to a column from Ben Thompson on Nvidia and Jensen Huang. A week later that whole situation has changed. But there was another bit in the same column I’ve been thinking about. Thompson wrote about the argument that it’s good for the U.S. to keep China hooked on chips from a U.S. company like Nvidia: Specifically, the Chinese government can only control the supply side, by spending money and making top-down imperatives; building an ecosystem, however, whether that be for AI spe
reason: Gruber digs into Ben Thompson's argument on chip export policy and whether keeping China hooked on US chips makes sense.
content_html:
Last week I linked to a column from Ben Thompson on Nvidia and Jensen Huang. A week later that whole situation has changed. But there was another bit in the same column I’ve been thinking about. Thompson wrote about the argument that it’s good for the U.S. to keep China hooked on chips from a U.S. company like Nvidia:

Specifically, the Chinese government can only control the supply side, by spending money and making top-down imperatives; building an ecosystem, however, whether that be for AI specifically, or semiconductors broadly, requires demand as well. Progress in models and systems and chips depends on a feedback loop between the user and the developer, or the customer and the manufacturer. The demand side, however, is much more short-term oriented than the Chinese government might prefer. The model companies’ concern is the other model companies: that means if they are distilling, we must distill too. If they are using Nvidia chips, then we must too. This matters up and down the stack, just as it has always mattered in technology, which really is different in this regard from almost every other industry.

A useful analogy is to consider the Internet. Why is it that country after country can profess a desire to have an indigenous alternative to the American tech giants, yet miserably fail in every attempt to generate it? It’s because the tech giants are only a click away! In this regard, China’s Great Firewall was one of the most brilliant geostrategic moves ever: by virtue of cutting off access to the American tech companies, China created the demand that pulled China’s own tech giants into existence. You need demand, not just desire.

This is why China itself is currently banning the import of Nvidia’s two-generations-behind H20 chips, after the Trump administration foolishly banned their import, only to reverse themselves while bragging about the reason to do so — i.e. keep China addicted to Nvidia. China is replaying the Great Firewall playbook: force its internal demand to use its much worse alternatives, because that is the only way those alternatives become better. And, in the long run, those alternatives, and the entire ecosystem that supports them, will flood the world.

This rings true. If the EU (to cite one very conspicuous example) wants to see indigenous alternatives to platforms like Facebook, Google search, and iOS, they should ban those platforms, like China does with foreign-controlled platforms it doesn’t like. But instead, what the EU is doing is punishing its own citizens by allowing those platforms to operate in the EU while forcing them to cripple their own features to comply with EU regulations. The EU strategy (such that it is) means that the EU gets no homegrown alternatives (because the existing platforms remain available, which extinguishes the demand to create alternatives), while foisting upon EU citizens worse versions of those platforms, because they’re saddled with EU-specific restrictions and missing features.

content_html:
Nvidia Newsroom:

Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

Well, the tech side was right and the political side (including me) was wrong. Perhaps because the AI/VC cadre had a better read on the Trump administration’s remaining political capital and their willingness to use it on this. President Trump, on his blog:

On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security.

I’m sure, under Huang’s chairmanship, they’ll get right on that.

This, after The New York Times reported over the weekend that Alice Huang, was, in fact, in regular contact with an official of China’s MSS for over a year, up through this fall.

title: John Siracusa launches Jetty Pro ↦
summary: My little auto-hiding palette features connections to file servers, SSH shortcuts, screen-sharing shortcuts, Keyboard Maestro macros, and more. A thousand beta builds later, John Siracusa has finally launched his new app, a dock-and-palette utility called Jetty Pro: I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. …
reason: John Siracusa finally ships Jetty Pro, a power-user Mac palette from one of your favorite writers.
content_html:
A thousand beta builds later, John Siracusa has finally launched his new app, a dock-and-palette utility called Jetty Pro:

I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to.

I’ve been using this app for months and I love it. It has very specifically filled a space in my Mac’s interface that has been empty since DragThing died in 2019, namely a palette full of arbitrary stuff like SSH connections, folders, macros, and URLs that I want to get to with a single click.

For a guy who has a reputation for liking things just so, you might think Jetty Pro does things only one way. That’s not true. One of the things John wants just so is for his apps to have a lot of user-configurable options. You can make palettes of various looks, with various behaviors, and have their behavior remain consistent or vary depending on what display you’re using.

(And yes, it is a thorough Dock replacement, so I can finally have a second Dock appear on the right side of my secondary display whenever I have it open.)

In John’s unsurprisingly detailed FAQ page he explains why the app is available only on a subscription basis—mostly, it’s because it will require a lot of maintenance due to its use of private Apple APIs. Those private APIs are also why it’s not available in the Mac App Store, but only direct from John.

Jetty Pro has a 14-day free trial, and then costs $10 for the first year. Oh, and there’s no non-Pro version of Jetty in the Mac App Store. John worked on one for a while, but it didn’t make sense. All the goodness of Jetty Pro is happening with John’s circumvention of Apple’s rules. He’s a rebel! And his attempt to slowly rebuild every feature of DragThing continues.

title: Subtitles everywhere in version 27 releases
summary: The kids, they love their subtitles. It was a minor moral panic a few years ago that The Youth were so lazy that they enabled subtitles on everything they watched so they didn’t have to listen, or some other nonsense.…
reason: Six Colors on how the version 27 OS releases put subtitles and captions everywhere.
content_html:
The kids, they love their subtitles. It was a minor moral panic a few years ago that The Youth were so lazy that they enabled subtitles on everything they watched so they didn’t have to listen, or some other nonsense.

Then the pandemic hit and, dear reader, I became The Youth. As apparently did a huge number of people. With divided attention and stress, and the realization that, hey, I’m aging, that I could get used to having onscreen captions, and that they wouldn’t distract me, we all enabled subtitles and mostly didn’t look back.

With the computing power formerly reserved for entire sci-fi planets now packed into each piece of Apple silicon, the company has brought machine learning to bear in its version 27 operating systems to provide live subtitles for video.

Speak up, sonny

Starting in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and tvOS 27, you can enable generated subtitles and captions. Remarkably, Apple didn’t create a capitalized term for this, partly, I think, because it wanted the feature to appear in parallel with encoded subtitles that are part of many TV shows, movies, and web-hosted videos.

Apple Intelligence is required on an iPhone, iPad, or Mac. With tvOS 27, the Apple TV has to be on the same network as an iPhone or iPad that has Apple Intelligence and is logged into the same Apple Account.

Here’s how to enable it:

  • On an iPhone or iPad: Go to Settings: Accessibility: Subtitles & Captioning and enable Closed Captions + SDH.
  • On an Apple TV: Follow the iPhone/iPad path above, then also enable Show Generated Subtitles.
  • On a Mac: Go to System Settings: Accessibility: Subtitles & Captioning: Prefer closed captions and SDH.

If you haven’t tweaked this setting area before, you should examine the additional settings, most of which are on by default on most platforms:

  • Languages don’t match: Phrased slightly differently in each operating system, this brings up subtitles automatically if your device language doesn’t match the encoded language of the video.

  • Show when muted: When you mute, subtitles appear automatically.

  • Show on skip back: If you use the skip-back feature to rewind slightly, subtitles appear for up to 30 seconds.

  • Apply across apps: On an iPhone, iPad, or Mac, you can preserve your subtitles on/off setting from one app to another. If you disable it, each app’s subtitles setting is uniquely preserved.

How this appears

In practice, the captioning works better than Siri keyboard dictation, which makes sense, as Apple should have access to all recorded audio tracks. It may have trained its machine-learning algorithms using that set of known examples, coupled with the feedback of encoded captions across many languages. There’s no better reinforcement learning than that. (But that is speculation on my part.)

When generated subtitles appear, Apple uses a unique icon at the beginning of each line that your device shows.

In the photo, you can see I got a little excited watching the BBC quiz program University Challenge when they asked a question about flong and stereotypes. But I was impressed that the generated captions correctly interpreted what I said.1

You can see this working across your apps and devices. For instance, I could watch a clip of Norm Eisen posted to Bluesky using the Indigo app, and have it captioned. Note that in the image below, the caption overlaps the chyron.2

You can create subtitle styles via the Style menu in Subtitles & Captioning, and access them from the subtitle menu in the video player. I created a much more opaque and larger version.

Note that subtitles only work when using Apple’s video player. Embedded videos that use a different player on a web page or within an app can’t access generated subtitles.

Generated subtitles have the greatest effect for things like the clip above and our personal videos: media that otherwise wouldn’t be captioned by a human being, but for which it can be useful to have text to read as an adjunct. With translation, this gives you access to video that would otherwise be incomprehensible.

I admit that subtitling can reduce focus on the thing you’re watching. But the tradeoff is understanding exactly what’s going on!

[Got a question for the column? You can email glenn@sixcolors.com or use /glenn in our subscriber-only Discord community.]

  1. It misspelled Ged as Gedd, but that’s unimportant. And it got Hunterian correct, a museum in Scotland. ↩
  2. But the flagon with the dragon has the brew that is true. ↩

title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
summary: This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press . Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it.

content_html:
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.

Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.

Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.

When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.

Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.

The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.

The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.

The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.

The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

title: This Is How To Give A Great Presentation: 5 Secrets From Neuroscience
summary: Okay, so you have to give a presentation at work… First of all, I’m sorry. I truly am. Public speaking is a punishment Dante forgot to include in “Inferno” because he lacked imagination. The thing I find weird is that people think presentations are terrifying because everyone’s staring at you. Wrong. They’re terrifying because nobody […] Reading this in a feed reader? reason: Practical, research-backed advice on giving better presentations, from a writer you've favorited.
content_html:
Mock dictionary entry for PowerPoint Prodigy (noun): the person who turns a 2-minute topic into a 40-slide presentation

Okay, so you have to give a presentation at work…

First of all, I’m sorry. I truly am. Public speaking is a punishment Dante forgot to include in “Inferno” because he lacked imagination.

The thing I find weird is that people think presentations are terrifying because everyone’s staring at you. Wrong. They’re terrifying because nobody is. The truly humiliating thing is that nobody cares.

Everybody in your audience has somewhere else they’d rather be. It’s like trying to perform “Hamlet” in front of a group of people who thought they were going to see a monster truck rally.

But you still want to give a great presentation. So what’s the secret?

Well, here’s where neuroscience comes in. Yeah, neuroscience, that smug, overachieving cousin of regular science. If you know how the brain works, maybe you can get your hostages audience to actually pay attention and learn something.

So let’s find out what neuroscience can teach us about giving a great presentation.

John Medina is a professor of bioengineering at the University of Washington School of Medicine. His wonderful book is “Brain Rules.”

Let’s get to it…

 

How To Start A Presentation: Lead With The Gist

Many people think presenting is merely conveying information.

“I’ll just present the data as written and they’ll follow along.”

Sure. And people watch celebrity breakups for sociological research.

Neuroscience research suggests something every good book and movie knows: if you don’t grab your audience in the opening moments, you will spend the rest of the hour speaking to a room of semi-conscious husks.

Medina is blunt: “If you are trying to get information across to someone, a compelling introduction may be the most important single factor in the success of your mission.”

So start with the gist of your talk. The big picture. The “Why should I care?” moment. None of that meandering preamble nonsense. Right out of the gate, punch them in the brain with your main point.

Medina says this provides a 40% boost in understanding. Without an early look at the big picture, people’s brains are left scrambling for coherence. You’re handing them puzzle pieces without showing them the box.

Then, present the information in a logical, hierarchical format. Key idea, details, next key idea. You want there to be an underlying structure they can follow, like a song, so you avoid the dreaded “Where is this going?” question.

(To learn how to overcome your fear of public speaking, click here.)

Okay, you’ve got their brains engaged. But now there’s a new problem we’re all too familiar with: attention spans…

 

The 10-Minute Rule: How To Keep An Audience’s Attention

A presentation is like a bank heist. You are on the clock from the moment you begin.

You have mere seconds to capture their attention. Accomplish that one? You’re still on borrowed time. Psychologist Wilbert McKeachie found that audience attention to a speaker consistently nosedives after 10 minutes.

So when composing your presentation, divide it into 10-minute chunks with a “hook” after every section to yank your audience back from the brink of unconsciousness and reset the clock.

Each hook is 1-2 minutes dealing with a single core concept. Use the other 8-9 minutes to dive into the details explaining it. Repeat.

What do the best hooks have in common? Four things:

  1. Emotion: Not optional. If you’re not moving people emotionally, you’re delivering verbal Valium. Humor counts as an emotion and thank God for that. (Will Eric tell a story about nearly mistaking a bidet for a drinking fountain in order to get the audience back? Eric will absolutely tell a story about nearly mistaking a bidet for a drinking fountain in order to get the audience back.)
  2. Relevance: If you just make a joke or tell a story about a lost puppy every ten minutes, the talk won’t cohere. The hook needs to be related. (Okay, maybe I won’t make the bidet joke.)
  3. Brevity: Hooks, done well, are powerful. But this can threaten to overwhelm what the talk is actually about. Two minutes, max.
  4. Storytelling: A short, relevant, emotional story is an excellent hook.

(To learn the 5 steps to presenting like a leader, click here.)

Okay, you grabbed their attention and you can hold it. But what about the substance of the presentation?

 

Make Them Understand Or They Won’t Remember

Emotion is vital, and it’s the part everyone loves to talk about. But unless you’re a motivational speaker, it’s secondary. Emotion is the DJ at a strip club. Plays an important part, sure, but it’s not really why anybody showed up.

You need to make them understand whatever it is your talk is about. If they don’t get it, they won’t remember it.

The secret? First, you must really understand the subject. Inside and out. You need to know why those numbers matter, what they mean, and how to explain them to someone who’s been actively avoiding numbers since high school.

A lovely side effect of being this prepared? Knowing your stuff cold is also where confidence comes from.

If you ever see me looking confident in public, please know one of two things is happening: I have dissociated completely, or I have to poop so badly that fear has been replaced by purpose. And before you say “Wow, that sounds like anxiety,” yes. Thank you. I’m aware. I live here.

But I’m extremely confident when presenting because I know the subject frighteningly well.

Which leads us to the other common problem: because you understand it, you assume everyone else will, too. This is so prevalent it has a name: “the curse of knowledge,” which sounds like a bad Harry Potter spell.

You can’t just show people a bunch of numbers and hope for the best. Tell them what those numbers mean for their actual day-to-day lives. How does it connect to what they already know?

“This results in an adjusted equivalency factor of 15% this quarter.”

Uh… should I be happy? Scared? Should I order a cake?

It’s your job to connect the dots, and explain why this matters. You need to be the Bob Ross of corporate presentations, painting little trees of meaning all over your slide deck.

Your audience is not going to do that work for you. Paint the picture. Show them where the squirrels live.

(To learn how to make your writing more persuasive, click here.)

But how do you make them understand if the topic isn’t inherently interesting?

 

Use Examples To Make It Memorable

If you want people to remember the things you’re presenting, use lots of examples. Without examples, you’re asking people to work. You think anyone wants to work during your presentation? HAHAHAHAHAHA. No.

Our brains are lazy. Brains love examples because examples do half the thinking for them. Using rich examples and connecting your info to stuff people already know produces “elaborate encoding” which increases remembering.

Nobody remembers the bullet points or the pie charts. They remember the stories and the absurd examples that make the abstract concrete.

People do love statistics they can share. And these make you, the presenter, look intelligent without having to actually be intelligent. Trust me; I’ve built a career based on this principle.

Turn each number into a scandalous love triangle between profit, loss, and the sultry, unpredictable mistress known as market volatility.

(To learn how to change someone’s mind, click here.)

What about the presentation itself? The style? The medium you use? Does it make a difference to the brain?

You better believe it does…

 

Use Visuals, Not Walls Of Text

Your gray matter remembers things better when multiple senses are involved. So incorporating images, audio, and video is neuroscience-approved.

Nearly half of your gray matter’s resources are devoted to processing visual information. Vision is, no doubt, the Freddie Mercury of the senses. It’s powerful and wears the tightest pants.

If possible, communicate more with pictures than with words. And if you dare use those sad stock photos of business people high-fiving in a conference room, I will personally attend your next presentation and heckle you into oblivion.

Don’t get too creative. We’ve all heard stories of someone using inappropriate images or videos, leading to them becoming famous in the worst possible way.

But there’s a reason that movies combine powerful visuals, great ideas, and music into the final product.

(To learn 6 more presentation techniques, click here.)

Okay, we’ve covered a lot. Time to round it up and we’ll learn the essential brain secret to effectively preparing for a talk…

 

Sum Up

Here’s how to give a great presentation:

  • How To Start A Presentation: Lead With The Gist: You’re standing in front of a room full of people who’ve barely had enough coffee to make their faces function properly. Give them the gist up front and a structure they can follow.
  • The 10-Minute Rule: How To Keep An Audience’s Attention: Assume you’re presenting for an audience of narcoleptics. Every ten minutes something notable needs to happen or they’re out.
  • Make Them Understand Or They Won’t Remember: Do not be a fact parrot. If you drone on about KPIs without explaining what a KPI is, the audience will assume it means “Kill Presenter Immediately.”
  • Use Examples To Make It Memorable: The human mind is not a sponge, despite what your kindergarten teacher claimed. It’s more like a sieve. Use rich, relatable stories to produce the lovely “Oh, now I get it” response.
  • Use Visuals, Not Walls Of Text: Are you putting up a slide that’s a wall of text? Then you deserve the collective groan you’re going to hear.

So how does the brain like you to prepare? It’s called state-dependent learning. Simply put: our ability to remember information is dramatically improved when we learn it in the same context we’re expected to recall it.

To the best of your ability, practice under the conditions in which you’ll present. Same amount of sleep, same amount of caffeine. Can you practice in front of a live person? Can you actually practice in the room you’ll be presenting in?

Recreate the vibe. Our brains are like method actors who insist on living in a cabin in the woods to really “get into the role” of a serial killer.

Can I offer one more tip, from lil ol’ me?

A lot of people think they need to seem impressive. Authoritative. This is an exhausting ambition. It also makes speaking much harder. You’re trying to communicate an idea while simultaneously operating a life-size puppet of yourself. No wonder you’ve forgotten what the next slide says.

I understand the impulse. I’d love to be effortlessly commanding. But think about someone you’ve actually enjoyed listening to. Chances are you remember their enthusiasm. A story they told.

Once you’ve done the hard work, once all the boxes are checked, be human. Once you know the material cold and you’ve replayed the talk over and over in your head like it’s the Zapruder film, focus on the passion and enthusiasm. Bring back the strip club DJ.

You’re allowed to enjoy the thing you’re talking about. It’s cool to care enough that it shows. Once you know your stuff, unguarded enthusiasm is welcome. And infectious.

Make them glad you came. Then leave before they’re glad you’re going.

content_html:
Strong winds will hit portions of our region, with thousands losing power.

In addition, heavy precipitation will reach our shores over the next week, hopefully easing some El Niño drought fears.

First, the winds.  

Seattle enjoys the most sophisticated wind prediction system in the nation, Seattle WindWatch, run at the UW and funded by Seattle City Light.  

Below is the maximum gust forecast for today (Tuesday) at 2 PM from WindWatch.  Gusts exceeding 60 mph over the eastern Strait of Juan de Fuca and along the coast.   Also, very strong winds on the northeast slopes of the Olympics.

That means some power outages. 


This strong wind event has long legs.  Below is the wind forecast for Wednesday evening.  More of the same, but with stronger winds along he coast.


So how do we understand this complex wind pattern?

The key wind driver is a deep low-pressure area well off our coast, as shown by the sea level pressure forecast for Tuesday morning (below).

With strong, cold high pressure inland, there is an intense east-west pressure difference between the coast and western Washington.

Strong pressure differences drive winds.


To understand the profound impacts of local terrain on winds in this situation, here is a plot of the pressures (isobars) and winds (colors) for Tuesday morning.

There is high pressure on one side of the Olympics and a trough of low pressure on the northeast side.  

This pressure pattern is produced by strong southerly (from the south) winds passing up and over the Olympics.  Air forced to rise by the Olympics cools by expansion, producing higher pressure.  Air sinking down he lee side warms by compression, resulting in low pressure.

The resulting intense pressure difference produces the powerful winds northwest of the Olympics.

 
There are also some moderately strong winds descending the western slopes of the Cascades from North Bend to Enumclaw.  SeaTac Airport will get a taste of this.
  
Here is Seattle: Seattle WindWatch is only predicting about 30-35 mph ( see below).  A few outages would be expected.  Thursday is the bigger threat than today.


Frustratingly, Seattle City Light told me that they don't have the funds to continue WindWatch. A shame, considering the important role it has played in ensuring City Light was prepared for strong wind events.   Time to buy a generator.

Winds along the coast are forced by the strong coastal pressure difference driven by the offshore low, as well as the low amount of drag over the ocean.  

What about precipitation?

Model forecasts are predicting serious rain over our region.  Reservoir-filling rain. Snowpack enhancing at higher elevations.

Below is the UW model's total precipitation forecast through Thursday afternoon.   

Wow. Up to 10 inches (yellow colors) in some locations.


The European AI model (the best long-range prediction by far) forecasts heavy amounts through December 7.  

This model, because it is low-resolution, is underplaying the amounts we would expect.


The predicted snowfall totals through the same period will make local ski enthusiasts smile:


Finally, there could be some minor coastal flooding, but the impacts will be minor compared to the winds and precipitation.

content_html:
Exclave Exploitation and the Camera Indicator Lights

It started with a single bug in one Exclave service that gave us a foothold on older devices. From there, an AI agent, working in GLxRunner, our hypervisor research environment, kept finding more bugs, until we had code execution on the newest devices as well. We will show how these bugs were combined to move from one Exclave to the next, and how the indicator light became the goal.

Finally, we will discuss what it takes on a modern Apple system to tinker with the indicator lights, and what this means for the protection Exclaves are meant to provide.

This is a forthcoming session at Black Hat.
