reason: Norway's NSM disclosed an Azure API Management flaw being used to target customer secrets, directly relevant to your Azure security work.
content_html:
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

"An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said. "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been."

The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses.

According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected.

"On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory.

"Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."

As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include -

  • Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers
  • Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers
  • Subscription keys
  • Tokens used to call direct management APIs

As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."

NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

title: Anatomy of Apple’s Personal Knowledge Graph
summary: Dario Pasquini and Michał Bazyli (Hacker News): Every Mac since macOS 13 ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, whom you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you […]
reason: A teardown of the daemons building a personal knowledge graph on every Mac, with privacy implications worth understanding.
content_html:
Dario Pasquini and Michał Bazyli (Hacker News):

Every Mac since macOS 13 ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, whom you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you do and when. In this post, we look into how this system works and give you a tool to peek into your own graph.

[…]

The closest thing to an official description is the man page (man 8 knowledgeconstructiond), and this is all you get[…]

[…]

To be fair, Apple’s own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. Also, we personally ran into it in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop.

[…]

The two daemons keep their work in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform, a directory of SQLite databases (fifty-one databases) stored in plaintext but located in a zone protected by TCC Full Disk Access.

There doesn’t seem to be anything really surprising here, but I hadn’t seen it laid out before.

title: Secure Exclaves and Ambient Sensing
summary: Apple (MacRumors): We recently introduced HomeView, which can recognize up to six people to deliver a rich and personalized experience. This capability relies on ambient sensing: using the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face. We have always believed features like this must be designed from […]
reason: Apple explains how Secure Exclaves protect HomeView's ambient sensing, squarely in your Apple security interests.
content_html:
Apple (MacRumors):

We recently introduced HomeView, which can recognize up to six people to deliver a rich and personalized experience. This capability relies on ambient sensing: using the microphone and camera to understand the surrounding environment and recognize an enrolled user’s voice and face. We have always believed features like this must be designed from the ground up to protect user security and privacy, and are now taking these protections even further, with a new security architecture in Apple silicon that’s purpose-built for ambient sensing. This work both benefits our newest features and strengthens the security of features we already ship, such as “Hey Siri” detection. Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks, while giving users a clear, reliable, and tamper-resistant signal whenever their sensors are fully active.

While ambient sensing relies on processing input from the camera or microphone, it must never record audio or video, nor expose it to the rest of the operating system.

[…]

To accomplish this, we have created Secure Exclaves: protected and compartmentalized runtimes used to process camera and microphone data separately from the rest of the system. Isolation features added across many core components of the silicon work in tandem to protect Secure Exclaves and keep them segregated from the rest of the system. Data that is processed and analyzed in a Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.

reason: Signal now blocks AI assistants from screen capturing chats, a notable shift in how secure messengers defend against on-device AI.
content_html:
Signal is extending screenshot-blocking protections to iPhones and supported Android devices to prevent AI assistants such as Siri and Gemini from capturing private conversations.


In its announcement, Signal said AI assistants can capture messages displayed on screen, potentially exposing conversations to processing outside the app. End-to-end encryption protects message delivery, but cannot prevent another app from reading messages visible on a recipient's device.

On iPhones running iOS 27, the new "Block ‌Siri‌ AI" setting is enabled by default in Signal version 8.37 or later. It blocks screenshots, screen recordings, and AI screen-reading. On supported Android devices running Signal 8.35.1 or later, screen security activates when an AI assistant attempts to read the screen.

iPhone users can disable the protection under Signal's Settings → Privacy → Block Siri AI, either permanently or for 10 minutes to take a screenshot. Apple also offers an Excluded Apps setting under Settings → Siri that prevents ‌Siri‌ from accessing selected apps.

Signal previously blocked Microsoft's Recall from capturing chats on Windows 11. It said equivalent screenshot blocking is unavailable on macOS and recommends excluding Signal from ‌Siri‌ there. The company is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft for better tools to keep app content out of AI systems.

title: The NVIDIA Bailout
summary: The US government helping to put Jensen Huang back in place is probably not going to help the anti-AI sentiment and narrative...
reason: Kafka on how the government's role in Huang's return could feed anti-AI sentiment.
content_html:
Jensen Huang is back. In the end, he was too big to fail. Or at least, that's what one person believed. And that person happens to be the President of the United States.

Reading over the myriad details of what happened here, I'm just not sure that anyone should be celebrating this news. I mean, if your NVIDIA holdings were a significant part of your net worth, then sure. And if you truly believe that Jensen Huang is AI Jesus in a leather jacket, then maybe. But the bigger picture here is one of both ridiculous interference in private company matters and, relatedly, a farcical degradation of corporate governance. Maybe such things no longer matter going forward. And given this situation, it's sort of hard to see how they do in the same way ever again.

All of that is to say there are some real vibes of the financial crisis here. Namely, the quick fix. The emergency "bailout". At first blush it feels like the stakes were much lower – this is just one tech company, not the entire US banking system, of course – but were the stakes actually that much different? There's a case to be made that if NVIDIA kept falling – not even failed, mind you, as the financials remain not just sound but exceptional – that it could have brought down the entire stock market with it. The catalyst that finally popped the "AI Bubble".

Maybe that would have happened or maybe NVIDIA, the stock, would have stabilized once investors fully digested the extraordinary situation. Clearly President Trump was worried that this would destroy his market narrative and potentially the positioning around continued AI leadership. Again, maybe that's fair, maybe it's not. But clearly many got in his ear, reportedly from Vice President JD Vance on down, that they needed to intervene. As to whether the intervention will actually work in the way they hope...

We'll get to that.

Of course, the Board didn't have to just roll over. But, if we're being honest, when the President of the United States calls into your Board meeting to suggest a new course of action, perhaps suggesting it will save the country, what else are you going to do? You can say you're going to stand on morals and principle, but come on, these are still human beings. Fallible, just like Jensen Huang.

That mixed with the fact that what was clearly their top choice to take over the top job, former NVIDIAN Rene Haas, seemingly turned down their offer to stay at ARM (while gaining a cushy new chairman role at majority owner SoftBank), left them in an even more precarious spot. Lisa Su probably wasn't coming to save the day. Tim Cook certainly wasn't. Johny Srouji? Maybe, but is he a big enough name to actually stabilize the situation and do Jensen-like things going forward?

Meanwhile, you had no less than Jeff Bezos saying publicly that they needed to hire internally – between this and the James Bond situation, is there no area in which this man won't meddle? CFO Colette Kress was thrown into an impossible situation as interim chief, and she obviously wasn't easing the Wall Street fears. Ian Buck's name kept being thrown out there, but there are clearly some reasons he wasn't immediately chosen – perhaps as simple as he didn't want to take on that level of responsibility, especially when his former leader was out there saying he'd be open to coming back.

I'm not trying to make excuses for the Board – they acted ridiculously here – but I'm trying to paint a picture of how this can all happen. It's not that hard to see, you don't even really need to squint. They had no good options and they risked being known as the people that brought down not just the most valuable company in the world, but potentially the entire AI industry and the entire US economy to boot.

That's probably overstating it, but when even just that potential fear is there, lingering, again... you see how this looks, right? They had to weigh all of this – while being leaned on by the President of the United States, no less – versus the threat of lawsuits on the other side. Those were going to come regardless. They already were!

And there was also a world where Jensen teamed up with other large investors to take them down regardless. That would have taken several months to execute, and it would have been complicated, but there was a path. Well, provided he wasn't charged with any actual crimes in the meantime.

That's obviously another key to all of this. The assurance – again, FROM THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES – that Jensen was not under investigation for any crimes against the country and would not be charged with any. I'm reminded of the "get out of jail free card" scene from Clear and Present Danger. "You don't... have one of these, do you Jack?" He does not, but Jensen seems to! As might the Board! Is this a de facto pre-pardon?!

The dealmaker-in-chief cut another one. He undoubtedly loved every minute of being the man in the middle here once again. He's not confessing, he's bragging!

Back to the Clear & Present Danger theme, "the press is gonna have a field day with this," notes President Bennett in the midst of a scandal. And the press certainly has here! We're once again in the situation where the tech press is pitted against tech insiders – namely NVIDIA investors and partners – for "causing" this scandal. Which is, of course, ridiculous. Jensen Huang caused this scandal by having sex with the leader of an NVIDIA partner and – seemingly now also admitted – his own employees, one of whom is reported to be a direct report of his.

And then lying about it. Multiple times. To the Board. To the public.

At the same time, it's undoubtedly also true that various factions – potentially even in the very same White House – wanted to see Jensen Huang neutralized. If not fully taken out, at least taken down a few rungs. Was there a political motivation in leaking some stories? I mean, come on, obviously. But again, it was Jensen that left this opening. Even if he was "honeytrapped" by Alice Huang, he presumably wasn't by his own employees that he was also apparently sleeping with!

Speaking of, the "spying" angle in all this continues to go back and forth. It always felt a bit overblown – or maybe just over-exaggerated in a big game of telephone – as if anything, she seemed less like James Bond and more like a potential asset that the Chinese government was seeking to leverage. And that was probably because she already had the Jensen relationship, not that she ensnared him into one. But the details here will obviously be under investigation for a while to come.

And that itself will start to spill into the public next week with the first set of Congressional hearings. Which will undoubtedly take this story in yet new and wild directions. And then when the Democrats fully come into power in Congress in January, the subpoenas are going to start coming out faster than NVIDIA chips off the shelves. If any discovery processes include emails or text messages... this whole thing could take some turbulent turns yet.

All of that is to say this isn't over, obviously. And while Jensen's return may have re-created $1T in value overnight, there's seemingly quite a few risks to the stock and company that didn't exist before – and this was and is the company at the center of the entire AI boom! It's not entirely clear that what the administration did in stepping in here wasn't just provide a stock pop – a sort of lifeboat in which some investors could bail after failing to when the ship was sinking without its captain. The captain is back, but is the ship fully intact?

Legal risks aside, it sure seems like China is no longer in any sort of equation for the company going forward – which, of course, means the deals Jensen had long lobbied for are no more.1 And if you assume there was some "shadow" market, which now goes to zero... there will be signs in the next couple of earnings.

Further, triumphant return or not, it's hard to see how Jensen now has any level of trust that he enjoyed previously on a number of fronts. Is TSMC still just going to be good doing "handshake" deals with him? Are other partners going to second-guess their reliance on his chips going forward? If nothing else, even more hedging feels prudent, if not necessary now.

Are NVIDIA shareholders going to continue to be fine with the "circular" financing arrangements that Jensen had been cutting left and right, helping to either inflate and/or prop up the AI market depending on how you look at it? Are regulators?

Lastly, I go back to the public. There's simply no way all of this helps the AI backlash, obviously. The question is how much it further hurts and/or inflames the situation. Again, I see a world in which this ordeal is held up as the new "bailout". Not exactly the same, but also not entirely different. A new symbol for a movement that Jensen had hoped to counter as the face and showman of AI.

So much for that.

title: Three Faster Ways to Board a Plane (that the Airlines Won’t Use)
summary: What science says is not what the airlines do
reason: Pogue on the science of faster airplane boarding and why airlines ignore it, a fun data-driven read.
content_html:
Seems like we board airplanes using the least efficient method possible.

I know, I know: This is news?

But does it just seem that way, or is it mathematically the worst way?

Today, I’ll answer that question. Seems like a perfect time, given that (a) this is the busiest air-travel week of the year, and (b) the whole air-traffic system seems to be breaking down anyway.

I know it’s on your mind. The last time I wrote about boarding flights (in the context of overhead bin usage), you guys went nuts in the comments—and many of you focused specifically on the boarding process.

Before we dive in, it’s important to understand the two human factors that slow down boarding.

  • Seat interference (industry term) is when the aisle person, already seated, has to get up to allow a later-arriving window or middle passenger in. Seat interference momentarily halts the entire boarding process.

  • Bin clumping (my term) is when passengers in rows 20–25 (for example) try to stow their bags in the bins simultaneously. One guy might stop at row 21, which holds up everyone trying to reach the rows past him. Boarding grinds to a halt until the people in each clot sort themselves out—and meanwhile, rows 1–19 and 26–50 are just sitting empty.

It stands to reason, then, that the fastest method is the one that minimizes those two factors.

The proposals

Over the years, people have studied a bunch of different boarding methods:

  • Front to back. Seat interference and bin clumping make the whole thing take forever. Your gut should tell you that this is the worst method.

  • By zones. On most airlines, including Delta, American, and Southwest, your boarding group is determined primarily by the price you paid: Pre-boarding, then first class and elites, then credit-card holders, then SkyMiles status, then the economy groups. Boarding efficiency is not a consideration.

  • Back to front seems like it would minimize bin clumping. This should be the best method, right?

  • Open seating. You board the plane like it’s a bus: You take any available seat once you’re on the plane. Until this year, Southwest used this system.

  • WILMA (Window, Middle, Aisle). Window-seat passengers board first, then middle, then aisle. Seat interference: eliminated.

  • Steffen method. In 2008, astrophysicist Jason Steffen ran hundreds of computer simulations to find the mathematically optimal boarding sequence. His solution: Back to front, window seats first, but also alternating rows. So: Even-numbered window seats first, then odd-numbered window seats. Then even-numbered middle seats, then odd-numbered middles. And so on. Multiple people are always stowing their bags simultaneously. No seat interference; no bin clumping.

What the science says

In theory—in computer simulations—here are the results, from slowest to fastest:

  • Front to back really is the slowest. Nobody would ever consider it—except for every airline that lets First and Business passengers board first.

  • Back to front. Well, here’s a surprise: It’s not really faster. “It seemed to be exactly the same as what I thought the worst way was, which would be boarding from the front of the plane to the back,” Steffen told me. You’ve still got seat interference; you’ve still got overhead-bin clumping. This method doesn’t address either one. (Alaska and Frontier do some back-to-front zoning.)

  • By zones. Really slow. It has all the drawbacks of a front-to-back design, because First and Business classes board first, blocking access to the rest of the plane. Basic passengers may get seat assignments only when they check in, so they get whatever seats are left—middle seats scattered around the cabin—which means another round of seat interference.

  • Open seating. Surprisingly fast. Measurably better than back-to-front, front-to-back, and zone boarding. Seat interference goes way down, because people eagerly take window seats first. They self-sort into a pseudo-WILMA configuration. Meanwhile, lots of people are stowing overhead bags simultaneously, all down the aisle.

  • WILMA (Window, Middle, Aisle). This method eliminates the seat-interference problem entirely.

  • Steffen method. On paper, this is the easy winner. Nobody’s waiting to stow their carry-ons, nobody has to get up to let somebody into their row. By Steffen’s calculations, the plane is ready to go in half the time compared with zone boarding, and 30 percent faster than open seating.

And now, the disheartening twist: No airline uses any of the three fastest methods. (Southwest gave up open seating this year.)

Why the hell not?

The human reality

Turns out a computer model can get you only so far. In the real world, three very human factors complicate, or even destroy, the advantages of the faster designs.

  • Grouping. The Steffen and WILMA methods require breaking up groups traveling together, like couples, families, and student groups. Every person has to stand in line, and then board, individually. No airline wants to tell a family of four that they have to board separately.

  • Confusion factors. The Steffen method requires passengers to stand in precise boarding order, 1 to 150 (or whatever). If anyone in the queue is out of sequence, they reintroduce seat interference and bin clumping, and the system breaks down. You’re just never going to get people to surrender their sense of individuality for the sake of communal faster boarding.

  • Money factors. Annnnnnd this is the big one. Boarding sequence is big money. People pay a premium to get on a plane first. (Although if you ask me, that priority is exactly backwards; wouldn’t you rather spend the least amount of time sitting on your plane?) This is why Southwest gave up open boarding: It’s simply more profitable to charge extra for earlier boarding.

On a “NOVA” show I hosted in 2013, we learned these points the hard way. The idea was to test the competing boarding systems in the real world.

Southwest Airlines donated a Boeing 737 and a gate at the Phoenix airport for the day. We rounded up 150 volunteers, hooked up a bunch of cameras, and invited two experts in plane-boarding systems: Doug Lawson, architect of Southwest’s open-boarding system (and, in his previous career as a paleontologist, finder of one of the largest flying animals that ever lived), and Jason Steffen himself.

You can watch the whole segment here. The gist is that Steffen’s method was faster than Lawson’s open seating—but even in this tightly controlled experiment, with a bunch of producers and experts handing out numbers and giving instructions, the Steffen method still broke down. We saw people ignoring their lineup order, thereby throwing a wrench into the whole precision machine. (Not shown: We actually had to re-do the whole Steffen experiment because people found it so confusing the first time.)

Today, the only major U.S. airline making any effort to speed up boarding is, believe it or not, United. Its system is based on WILMA, although it’s heavily diluted. It kicks in only in boarding groups 3 and higher (pre-boarding, First and Business, and credit-card holders still board first); families and groups still board together; and most Basic Economy passengers board last, even after the aisle people are already seated, so you get a lot of seat interference at the end. Even so, United says that its system gets you on your way two minutes faster.

Despite all of this effort, all of this science, and steadily growing passenger complaints, the average time to board an airplane has gone up over the last 20 years. In part, that’s by design. The airlines have introduced checked-bag fees, which encourage more people to bring carry-ons, which creates more competition for overhead-bin space, which makes people willing to pay more to board early. If we check our bags, we pay; if we carry them on, we pay to make sure there’s room. We lose either way. It’s sheer brilliance.

The bottom line: The airlines have optimized the boarding process—just not for efficiency.

Happy Thanksgiving, everyone.

title: Skipper, Tripod, and finding apps that fit
summary: We live in a world with so many monolithic apps and services, dominated by giant companies. So one of my favorite things is to explore little software niches that haven’t been captured by the major players.…
reason: Six Colors explores small, well-crafted apps that fit niches the big platforms ignore.
content_html:
We live in a world with so many monolithic apps and services, dominated by giant companies. So one of my favorite things is to explore little software niches that haven’t been captured by the major players. Instead of one or two pretty samey apps, you can end up with a whole forest of wild variations on the theme, each fueled by developers making specific choices about how to present information and serve users.

When I compare these apps, I realize that there’s really no right or wrong—there are just choices, some of which might work for me, some of which won’t. I’m not offended when an app isn’t made for me, but I can be delighted when an app does slide perfectly into my life.

After a year of using Television Time (not to be confused with the now-defunct TV Time) to log my TV viewing and (more importantly) let me keep track of what we’re watching next and what we’d like to get to next, I discovered an app that just served me better.

That’s Skipper, Yoav Zoldan’s new app, available for $30/year or $3/month. What sold me on it is that its primary screen is a list of shows I’m watching with the next episode marked, sorted in a way that makes sense to me. I only want to interact with the app in a handful of ways: seeing what to watch next, checking the box indicating that we watched it, and occasionally searching to add a show that I might be interested in watching next.

Television Time required more swiping around and entering detail views, and one thing I’ve discovered about myself is that I prefer apps that are optimized to present all the information I want in one place, and which limit the number of swipes and taps required to navigate around. Skipper hit that sweet spot for me—your mileage, of course, may vary.

Skipper has a lot of other features, including a very clever one that compares your watch list to your streaming service subscriptions and can nudge you to drop that service you’re not actually using, complete with a calendar of when shows you watch will be returning. (I know, I know, I shouldn’t have subscribed to BritBox. I have no time to watch it!)

It’s not entirely accurate—it doesn’t seem to understand that I watch sports on YouTube TV and things that are not shows on YouTube Premium—but it’s a smart feature that could help a lot of people who are not inveterate streaming subscription sickos like me.

Just as there are many TV-tracking apps, there are many, many podcast apps. I’ve been using Overcast for ages, and it just fits into how I want to listen to podcasts. I spend as little time as possible picking what to listen to (there’s my optimization streak again) and have Overcast configured to give me that.

But there have been other podcast apps that serve other, equally valid, points of view. Castro really made its name by not just offering a beautiful interface, but a clever “triage” system that brings new episodes into an inbox. Then the user manually decides what’s worth adding to the play queue. Clearly that approach clicked with a lot of people, making Castro a fan favorite even through its ongoing business challenges and different owners.

Which brings me to an impressive new podcast app that’s been designed to appeal especially to Castro fans: Ben Rice McCarthy’s Tripod. Ben is a really talented designer, and the app looks gorgeous and works well. It’s built around the same Inbox concept as Castro, so Castro users will feel right at home. I got to beta test Ben’s app for a while, and was incredibly impressed—especially at how it works on the iPhone Duo.

That all said, I am just not the target audience for Tripod—and that’s okay. The way Overcast works for podcasts is the way I want to work. Quite frankly, the idea of having another Inbox to check does not fill my heart with joy, even if the podcasts found therein would bring me that joy. That’s on me, not on Ben, and not on Tripod.

So if you watch TV like me, you should try Skipper. And if you’re not like me, you should try Tripod. That’s the beauty of these app niches; they don’t have to be all things to all people, they just need to find their audience and serve them well.

title: How to make a lovable city
summary: Camillo Sitte made the blueprint for beautiful cities. Here are his five principles.
reason: Camillo Sitte's five principles for beautiful cities, a thoughtful design and progress read.
content_html:
Everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.

The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.

Sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.

Sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.

Anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte showed, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.

Share

Create enclosed spaces

The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.

While the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.

The picture above shows the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.

Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.

London’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.

An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.

Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above shows Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.

Squares should not be too large

If a square is too large, it loses its sense of enclosure, and its buildings look strangely diminished by their surroundings. Sitte provided a rule of thumb in sizing squares: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it. The pictures above show two examples of over-large squares: the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest. Both feel demoralizingly vast, with the monumental buildings they are meant to showcase (Madrid Cathedral, and Budapest’s Hall of Art) dwindling to visual insignificance on the horizon, so that they resemble doll’s houses. In both squares, the buildings are so miniaturized that they no longer seem like enclosing walls, leaving the visitor exposed in a huge open space. This problem could be solved by making the buildings much taller, but although the square would then feel enclosed, the buildings would have become terrifyingly huge, as if meant for giants rather than human beings (the courtyard of Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris is an example of this pitfall in the wild).

Subscribe to print

Some of the world’s most famous squares are, in fact, far too large. St Peter’s Square in the Vatican, seen above, was designed by the famous artist Bernini, and it does indeed look impressive in drone footage. For human visitors, however, it is an exhausting place, overwhelming without being impressive. The Basilica looks small and stubby, exactly the opposite of the desired effect. On a summer’s day, the vast, unshaded space becomes relentlessly inhospitable, and visitors huddle under the colonnades for shelter.

By contrast, the small square in front of the Pantheon in Rome exemplifies the features Sitte prized. It is impossible to fully capture its feeling of enclosure in a two-dimensional photograph, but some sense of the intimacy of the space is apparent in the pictures above, which show how this magnifies the Pantheon. The Pantheon is a smaller building than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, but it is much bigger relative to the square. This allows it to retain its dignity, despite the fact that the level of the street has risen by 1.3 meters since Antiquity, swallowing the steps that originally led up to the entrance.

Symmetry is overrated

At the time Sitte was writing, many planners believed that harmonious spaces should have regular, symmetrical plans, an idea which remains influential today. In English we even use the confusing word ‘square’ for any enclosed public spaces, whatever their shape.

Sitte rejected this, believing that symmetrical spaces do not necessarily feel harmonious at ground level, and that asymmetry is not generally disharmonious at all. The pictures above show the perfectly symmetrical Place Vendôme in Paris. Seen from a satellite, it is visually striking and certainly neater than an irregular space. Its chamfered plan supposedly inspired the design of Chanel’s No 5 perfume bottle. Pedestrians, however, generally do not stand at the exact point at which the objective balance of the buildings is reflected in their field of vision: the various points and angles from which they do experience it may even make it feel quite awkward.

Above is the Piazza delle Erbe, a market square in Verona. This ‘square’ has an odd shape, an elongated and slightly wonky pentagon. Nobody is likely to model perfume bottles on it. But at human level, this does not matter as pedestrians can never take in all five sides at once, and so its irregular form is barely even visible. For the most part, the irregularities are ‘seen only on paper’, and to the extent they are visible, they are not experienced as imperfections. Sitte argued that they in fact serve to subtly arouse visual interest, and also create happy recesses that can host resting places, statues, or other public art.

Subscribe to print

Move monuments to the edges

If you were putting an ornament in your living room, you would be very unlikely to stand it in the middle of the carpet. It would get in the way, break up the space, and might well look lost and isolated. Nor would you place it in front of one of the room’s main features, like the fireplace. It would block the view of the fireplace, and the fireplace would be a disagreeably busy backdrop. Almost certainly, you would put it against the wall, preferably a relatively neutral wall to create a calm background.

Sitte thought the same considerations applied to the placing of sculptures, fountains, and other monuments in outdoor spaces. Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares, where they would block natural routes, break up the space, and look isolated and diminished. Nor should they be placed on axes with key buildings, where they block the view of the architecture. Instead they should line the sides, where they can stand out against relatively neutral backgrounds.

This was implicitly understood in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance, and Sitte illustrates his book with examples from all three periods. Above, for example, is the Piazza della Signoria in Florence. The numerous statues line the sides of the square, leaving the center free for people to pass through or mill about. This is advantageous for the statues too: Michelangelo’s David (today a replica, since the original was moved indoors) stands out splendidly against the plain masonry walls of the Palazzo Vecchio.

Later planners became fascinated by the apparent neatness of centering statues. Above is the Victoria Memorial in London. The Memorial stands on the main axis of the Mall, blocking the view of Buckingham Palace behind it. This is not advantageous for the Memorial either, whose outline clashes confusedly with the complex detailing of the building. If you search through pictures of the Memorial, you will notice that most photographers picture it from an awkward oblique angle, the least bad way to capture both the monument and the central pavilion of the palace.

Isolating statues against the sky is not much better. A bronze cast of David was later placed on the Piazzale Michelangelo, at the center of a wide square with stunning views over Florence. The statue is enormous, over five meters tall, but it looks strangely miniaturized in its location. Sitte remarked that contemporary tourists often came away with the drastically false impression that it was life-sized. We judge size partly by comparison, and when an object is isolated from comparators, its size becomes harder to assess. This is why the backdrop of a wall can make sculpture look bigger and grander by providing a constant visual key.

In Sitte’s view, the plain edge of a small square was not only an acceptable site for a statue, but the best one. Sitte disliked museums, which he called ‘art prisons’, and thought that only people with a ‘special mental preparation’ could enjoy art under their ‘morbid influences’. The Sittesque city would be one that teemed with art, but woven into the urban fabric as an adornment of ordinary civic life.

Share

Buildings need context

Sitte’s view on buildings was similar. Nineteenth-century architects tended to place major public buildings in the middle of squares, judging that this gave them greater dignity. Sitte thought this ‘pedantic, futile modern practice’ destroyed the square and squandered the opportunity to frame the public building with vernacular architecture. He pointed out that many historic cities were in fact designed along the lines he proposed. Of the 255 churches of Rome, 41 adjoined other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three, and two on all four. Only six were freestanding, two of them modern churches of expatriate Protestant communities.

The most striking examples of this arose when nineteenth-century governments actually demolished the vernacular buildings that surrounded historic monuments. This practice, often known by its French name dégagement, was surprisingly common: nineteenth-century planners thought that it displayed the monuments better. It provides a useful experiment on the effect of freestanding versus adjoined monumental architecture.

For example, Notre Dame Cathedral was formerly approached through a narrow street called the Rue Neuve Notre Dame. The street was demolished by the government planner Haussmann in the nineteenth century to create the Parvis Notre-Dame, a large square that the cathedral still faces today. Haussmann intended to improve the view of the cathedral, but the effect is the opposite. The vernacular fabric formed a visual frame, defining and concentrating views onto the facade. It provided scale, making the cathedral look larger by contrast to the ordinary buildings around it. It also prevented visitors from seeing the whole facade until they were very close, close enough that it towered up terrifically before them. Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.

Sitte thought that cities should move in the opposite direction. The Votive Church in Vienna was built in the 1870s on what Sitte described as a ‘desolate monster plaza’ that was ‘intolerably exposed to high wind, inclement weather, heat and dust, as well as to the din of the streets, and the incessant clanging of trams.’ The church does indeed have an awkward and lonely feeling. Sitte thought that the architecture of the building was actually very good, and that the defects in its effect were entirely the fault of its location. He proposed building up regular urban fabric on most of the ‘monster plaza’, defining three small squares with well-framed views onto the church. Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.

Another way to understand this contrast is to look at whole cities planned on Sittesque and anti-Sittesque principles. The pictures below show Padua and Washington DC. It is as though a figure-ground switch has taken place: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings. Monumental buildings in Washington sit alone on their city blocks, untouched by vernacular fabric. Monumental buildings in Padua constantly link up with vernacular fabric to shape small, sheltered spaces from which they can be properly enjoyed.

The rise, fall, and rise of Camillo Sitte

The Art of Building Cities was an immediate success, landing, in the words of Sitte’s English translator Charles T Stewart, ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’. Within a year of publication it had prompted the redrawing of urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and Sitte was being approached by town officials seeking his advice on their own plans. By Sitte’s death in 1903, advocates of his ideas were to be found in prestigious positions in cities including Munich, Berlin, and Vienna, either teaching or as official city architects.

Subscribe to print

Two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate the effect of Sittesque ideas on urban planning. In the nineteenth century, Helsinki followed a neoclassical grid plan, with straight streets meeting at right angles. In the early twentieth century, it switched dramatically to a Sittesque approach, introducing curving streets, turbine squares, T-junctions, and asymmetrical spaces. The resulting neighborhood is full of pleasing, characterful spaces and unexpected ‘old town’ effects, even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor.

But Sitte’s influence was curiously short-lived. In the decades following Sitte’s death in 1903, European urban design came to be dominated by the modernist movement. Everything that Sitte hated about nineteenth-century planning was vastly amplified in modernism. With honorable exception, the modernists treated public space as merely whatever was left over after the buildings had been placed, and had no sympathy with Sitte’s approach of treating spaces as primary and shaping the buildings around them. Instead of lining the edge of a city block with buildings (a ‘perimeter block’) they preferred to orient all blocks in the same direction (‘parallel blocks’), often with a seemingly arbitrary angle to the street. Sitte had decried the gridiron blocks of the nineteenth century for the weakly defined spaces they created. But by twentieth-century standards, the straight ‘corridor streets’ of the nineteenth century look comparatively Sittesque.

Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.

Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘New Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. But the Sittesque revival goes far beyond this. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.

Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.

title: Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code Integrity
summary: A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday. The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked
reason: James Forshaw shows a one-bit change in .NET files bypassing Windows code integrity, classic deep security engineering.
content_html:
A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398.

Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared.

VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework.

The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face.

The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects.

To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis.

Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox."

The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host.

The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image.

The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it.

"This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced.

The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet.

Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights.

The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE.

What to patch

On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it.

.NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694.

Flaw Affected Fixed in
CVE-2026-87268 (VirtualBox) VirtualBox 7.2.16, Windows hosts Oracle's September update, build 7.2.18
CVE-2026-108398 (.NET Framework) .NET Framework 4 on Windows, UMCI case tested on Windows 11 S Mode October 13 update, per-version KB

Forshaw first presented the Windows code-integrity bypass at the 44Con conference in September, having judged it fell outside Microsoft's rules for what gets fixed. After .NET developers told him the behavior he had counted on was accidental, he reported it in late September. The fix arrived in October's Patch Tuesday, less than a month later.

title: Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.
